630.bp: A knowledge graph is a store of connected facts: things are nodes, relations are links, and types or classes describe what kinds of things and links are allowed. A company, search engine, scientific database, or public data portal may use this structure to combine facts from many sources. The hard practical question is not only whether a graph contains many facts, but whether the graph is still healthy as it grows. Are related parts tied together or split into islands? Can users travel from one fact to another through meaningful links? Has the organizing scheme become too deep, too shallow, or inconsistent? MetriKG serves the maintenance side of this world. It is a web application for profiling static and evolving knowledge graphs from RDF files or SPARQL endpoints. Its purpose is to turn a large connected knowledge store into measurements that help people monitor quality, consistency, and interpretability over time.
630.wh: The difficulty is that graph quality is not visible from a single fact. A fact can be correct by itself while the graph around it becomes confusing. One part may grow dense while another becomes isolated. A new class may be added to the schema, meaning the organizing rules of the graph, but the actual data may not follow that new shape. Existing evaluation methods, as described in the abstract, often look at static graphs or track evolution only at the data level. That misses a second layer of change: the schema can also evolve. If the graph says what entities exist but quietly changes what types, hierarchies, or relation patterns are expected, then users may trust a map whose rules have shifted underneath them. MetriKG is hard because it must summarize both surface facts and deeper organization without reducing everything to one vague quality score.
630.naive: A smart beginner might load the graph, count how many facts it has, count how many entity types appear, and compare those totals across two dates. If the counts rise, the graph looks healthier. If some links disappear, it looks worse. That approach fails because size is not structure. A graph can gain many facts while becoming less connected. It can keep the same number of classes while making the class hierarchy deeper and harder to interpret. It can add data that obeys old rules poorly, or change schema rules while the data-level counts look stable. Simple counts tell that something changed, but not what kind of change happened or whether it threatens cohesion, connectivity, classification, or later use.
630.ap: MetriKG's central move is to treat a knowledge graph like an object that can be profiled from several angles rather than judged by one headline number. The application accepts graphs either as RDF files, which are files of subject-relation-object statements, or through SPARQL endpoints, which are query services for asking a graph what it contains. It then computes a broad set of metrics for both static graphs and graphs observed over time. Some metrics describe data-level structure, such as how connected or cohesive the graph is. Others describe schema-level structure, such as inheritance depth, meaning how many layers sit between broad classes and more specific classes. The important design choice is the pairing of levels. MetriKG does not only ask whether the facts changed. It also asks whether the rules and categories that give those facts meaning changed.
630.mech: The mechanism begins with an input knowledge graph. If the user provides an RDF file, MetriKG reads the stored statements directly. If the user provides a SPARQL endpoint, it queries the graph through the endpoint instead. From there, the application separates two views. The data-level view looks at the concrete fact network: which entities are present, which relation links connect them, and how those links create connected regions or isolated pieces. The schema-level view looks at the organizing layer: what classes, relation types, and inheritance paths define the kinds of facts the graph is meant to hold. For a static graph, MetriKG computes metrics that summarize the current shape. Cohesion asks whether related pieces appear to hold together. Connectivity asks whether the graph provides usable paths across entities rather than disconnected islands. Inheritance depth asks how tall or layered the type hierarchy has become. For an evolving graph, the same kinds of measurements can be repeated across time points. The output is not a prediction or generated answer. It is a profile: a multi-dimensional record that supports classification, comparison, and temporal monitoring of graph structure and meaning.
630.math: The main mathematical idea is measurement of structure. A graph is a mathematical map made of points and links. In this paper, the points are knowledge-graph entities or schema elements, and the links are factual relations or organizing relations such as class inheritance. Once the graph is seen as a map, quality questions become measurable questions. Connectivity counts whether paths exist between places on the map and how fragmented the map is. Cohesion measures whether pieces that should belong together form tight regions instead of being scattered. Inheritance depth measures a hierarchy by counting how many parent-child layers separate general categories from specific ones. Temporal monitoring adds a sequence idea: the same measurements are taken at different moments so change itself becomes something that can be compared. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. A metric deliberately compresses a huge graph into a number or small set of numbers, which makes comparison possible but can hide the local reason behind a change. The math fits MetriKG because graph maintainers need repeatable, comparable signals of structure, not only hand inspection or isolated examples.
630.dots: MetriKG sits in the repo's knowledge-graph family because it handles the trust problem behind connected facts. Many neighboring papers use knowledge graphs for question answering, recommendation, retrieval, rule mining, causal explanation, or dynamic reasoning. Those systems depend on the graph being coherent enough that following links gives useful evidence rather than confusion. MetriKG does not itself retrieve answers or complete missing facts; it profiles the map those methods may rely on. It is especially close to temporal knowledge graph reasoning papers such as DSTAG and Dual History Enhancement, which treat facts as changing over time. Those papers ask how to predict or reason from change, while MetriKG asks how to measure and monitor the changing graph itself. It also connects to the network concept in the repo: links carry evidence only when the map's structure is meaningful. Profiling is the quality-control branch of the same broader problem.
630.ww: The approach works because many graph failures leave structural traces before they appear as obvious wrong answers. If a graph becomes fragmented, connectivity measures can reveal that users or downstream systems may no longer travel smoothly from one area of knowledge to another. If related entities stop forming cohesive regions, the graph may be mixing sources, relations, or categories in a way that weakens interpretation. If inheritance depth grows sharply, the schema may be becoming more complex, which can help precision but can also make the graph harder to understand and maintain. Tracking both data and schema matters because the two layers can disagree. Data may expand while the schema stagnates, or the schema may change while old data remains shaped by earlier assumptions. Repeating these measurements over time turns maintenance into comparison: instead of relying on a person's memory of the graph, MetriKG gives a consistent set of signals that can show drift, growth, fragmentation, or reorganization.
630.po: The payoff is a practical monitoring tool for people who build or maintain knowledge graphs. MetriKG gives them a web-based way to evaluate graphs from RDF files or SPARQL endpoints and inspect multiple dimensions of graph health, including cohesion, connectivity, and inheritance depth. That enables systematic profiling of a single graph, classification of graphs by structural and semantic properties, and temporal monitoring as graphs evolve. The abstract also says the application is open-source and publicly available, which matters because profiling tools are most useful when teams can inspect, reuse, and adapt them to their own graph stores.
630.limits: The abstract establishes what MetriKG computes, but it does not prove that the chosen metrics catch every important quality problem. A graph can score well on connectivity while containing wrong facts, stale relations, or misleading links. A schema can have reasonable inheritance depth while still using unclear class names or domain assumptions. The method assumes that RDF files or SPARQL endpoints expose enough of the graph and schema to measure them faithfully. It also assumes repeated snapshots are comparable over time. The abstract does not specify evaluation datasets, user studies, runtime costs, or thresholds for deciding when a metric value is good or bad.

631.bp: A cloud datacenter is a large shared machine room where many customers rent computing power at the same time. Each server has local memory, but some machines need more fast memory than they physically own while others have memory sitting idle. A disaggregated memory system tries to turn memory into a shared pool reachable over the datacenter network. Remote Direct Memory Access, or RDMA, is the fast network mechanism that lets one machine read or write memory on another machine with little CPU involvement. Wiseswap serves this setting: a cloud provider wants remote memory to feel dependable enough for real tenants, not just for a clean experiment. The paper focuses on swap operations, where a machine moves memory pages out and later needs them back. If those operations arrive late, applications stall. The practical question is how to share remote memory across tenants while keeping delay-sensitive memory traffic predictable, fair, and efficient when other RDMA applications are also using the same network.
631.wh: The hard part is that the shared memory pool is not separate from the rest of the cloud. It rides on the same datacenter fabric as other RDMA traffic. A tenant running a large transfer can create an elephant flow, meaning a long or heavy stream that occupies links and queues for a while. Another tenant may then issue a small but urgent memory swap request and be forced to wait behind traffic that is not urgent. Existing designs, according to the abstract, make three simplifying assumptions: they overlook interference from co-located RDMA applications, treat the network topology too simply, and do not provide elastic service-level objective guarantees. A service-level objective is a promise about acceptable behavior, such as delay staying below a target. The tension is therefore three-sided: prioritize urgent swap traffic without unfairly crushing user traffic, choose routes based on the actual fabric state rather than an ideal map, and change resource allocations as workloads fluctuate.
631.naive: A smart beginner might build a remote-memory pool and send swap traffic over RDMA using fixed paths and fixed resource settings. The system could assume that RDMA is fast enough, that the network fabric has enough capacity, and that tenants will mostly share without creating serious interference. It might also give every RDMA flow similar treatment because treating everyone the same sounds fair. This breaks as soon as tenants behave differently. A large background flow and a short urgent swap request have very different consequences if delayed, but equal treatment puts them in the same line. Fixed paths can keep using congested links even when other paths are clear. Fixed memory-service settings waste resources during light load and miss delay targets during bursts.
631.ap: Wiseswap's core move is to make disaggregated memory aware of the datacenter network while it is running. Instead of treating remote memory as a simple storage extension, it treats each memory access as traffic that must compete for paths, priority, and resources. The first part is preemption-enabled isolation: a low-overhead kernel mechanism uses RDMA WAIT and ENABLE primitives to let latency-critical swap operations move ahead of user-space RDMA flows while still preserving tenant fairness. The second part is adaptive fabric path selection: the kernel gathers latency telemetry, meaning fresh measurements of how slow different paths currently are, and sends memory traffic through less congested routes. The third part is feedback-directed autoscaling: the system watches workload changes and tunes disaggregated-memory parameters so it can meet strict service targets without keeping excess resources reserved all the time.
631.mech: The mechanism begins when a cloud workload needs memory beyond what its local server can comfortably provide. Its swap operations become requests to remote memory over RDMA. At the same time, other tenants may be running their own RDMA applications, some of which produce heavy network flows. Wiseswap sits in the kernel, the operating-system layer close enough to scheduling and network paths to act before application-level code can react. First, it distinguishes latency-critical swap operations from ordinary user-space RDMA flows. Using RDMA WAIT and ENABLE primitives, it can pause or release lower-priority traffic so urgent swap requests are not trapped behind longer transfers. Second, it probes the fabric from inside the kernel and records current latency along possible paths. That measurement is not a permanent truth about the network; it is a live signal used to avoid links that are currently congested. Third, the system uses feedback from workload behavior to adjust DMS-specific parameters. The abstract does not list those parameters, so the safe reading is that they are resource-allocation controls inside the memory-disaggregation service. The output is not a new prediction label or ranking. It is a running control decision: which traffic gets priority, which path carries memory requests, and how much resource the service allocates while trying to keep SLOs and reduce waste.
631.math: The main mathematical ideas are scheduling under priorities, routing on a changing network, and feedback-based optimization. Scheduling starts from a queue: several pieces of work want service, but only some can move first. The mathematical question is not simply who arrived first, but what cost is created by delay. A swap request can stall an application, so its delay cost is high; a long user-space RDMA flow may tolerate brief waiting. Routing treats the datacenter fabric as a map of links and switches, where each possible path has a current price such as measured latency. Choosing an uncongested path means comparing those prices and sending traffic where the expected waiting cost is lower. Feedback-based optimization means defining what counts as bad - SLO violations, high tail latency, low throughput, or wasted resources - and repeatedly changing controllable settings when measurements show the current choice is poor. The tradeoff is speed versus fairness versus resource use. Giving every urgent request absolute priority could harm other tenants. Reserving too much capacity could satisfy latency but waste memory and network resources. Wiseswap's math fits because the problem is not a static memory lookup; it is a control problem where routes, queues, and workloads keep changing.
631.dots: This paper belongs with the conference's efficiency and scalability work because it asks how to make a desirable system affordable under real load. Like other resource-aware systems in the repo, the scarce thing is not only compute; it is memory capacity, network bandwidth, queueing delay, and reserved headroom. It also connects to the network concept: the datacenter fabric is a graph of machines, switches, and paths, and evidence about congestion must guide where traffic should travel. The optimization connection is direct as well. Wiseswap repeatedly chooses settings and routes based on measured badness, especially latency and resource overhead. It sits near cloud QoS work such as adaptive bandwidth guarantees, but its object is more specific: remote memory traffic whose delay can pause a running application. It also has a fairness thread, because multi-tenant clouds must protect one tenant from another without turning priority into permanent privilege.
631.ww: The approach should work better than the naive design because it attacks the actual causes of delay instead of assuming they will not appear. If co-located RDMA traffic interferes with swap operations, then isolating swap traffic at the kernel level addresses the queue where the harm happens. WAIT and ENABLE primitives matter because they are close to the RDMA mechanism itself; they can shape traffic without waiting for each application to cooperate. If the fabric has multiple possible paths, then congestion is not just a property of the whole network but of particular links and routes at a particular time. Live latency probing lets the system use that unevenness rather than suffer from it. If workloads fluctuate, fixed resource settings are almost guaranteed to be wrong some of the time. Feedback-directed autoscaling uses recent behavior as a correction signal, increasing support when the service risks missing SLOs and reducing waste when demand falls. The reported throughput gains and tail-latency reductions under contention are consistent with this causal story.
631.po: The payoff is a version of disaggregated memory that is closer to cloud deployment conditions. The abstract reports that Wiseswap improves throughput by 1.3 to 2.4 times and reduces tail latency by 57 to 73 percent under contention compared with prior solutions. In practical terms, that means tenants can use remote memory with fewer extreme slow requests when other RDMA traffic is present. The cloud provider also gets a better resource tradeoff: it can pursue stringent service targets while avoiding unnecessary reserved capacity through feedback-directed autoscaling.
631.limits: Several assumptions must hold. Kernel-level control must be deployable in the target cloud stack, and RDMA WAIT and ENABLE behavior must be available and low overhead enough to help rather than add delay. Latency telemetry must reflect the paths memory traffic will actually experience; stale or noisy probes could route traffic badly. The fairness claim depends on how priority is bounded, since urgent swap traffic could otherwise crowd out ordinary RDMA flows. The abstract reports evaluation under contention, but it does not prove behavior for every topology, tenant mix, failure mode, parameter choice, or adversarial tenant deliberately shaping traffic to exploit priority rules.

632.bp: A phone, camera, or wearable can now carry a strong visual model, but the model was usually trained before it ever sees the place where it will be used. That matters because visual tasks are not only about object names. A model deployed in a factory, clinic, warehouse, classroom, or outdoor scene must deal with the light, background, camera angle, clutter, and visual habits of that environment. Few-shot learning is meant for exactly this pressure: the device may receive only one or a handful of labeled examples for a new task. Glasses serves the practical need of making those few examples count more. The paper focuses on visual models based on ViT backbones, meaning image models that process an image as many small pieces and combine their evidence. Its setting is edge deployment, where the device has limited computation, while the cloud has more samples and stronger machines.
632.wh: The hard part is that the device needs local adaptation before it has much local teaching data. A pretrained visual model carries broad visual knowledge, but it may treat a new deployment environment as slightly foreign. The same object can look different under a new camera, lighting condition, background texture, or viewpoint. If the model cannot adjust to those environmental habits, then one-shot or five-shot learning starts from the wrong visual assumptions. The obvious fix is to fine-tune the model before deployment using examples from the target environment. The abstract says that is usually infeasible because environment-specific samples are unavailable before the model is deployed. The second constraint is device cost. Fully updating a large backbone on an edge device can be too slow or heavy. The paper therefore faces a timing problem and a resource problem at once: adaptation is needed after deployment, but the device alone cannot afford large tuning and does not have labels.
632.naive: A smart beginner might leave the pretrained backbone unchanged and train only a small task head from the few labeled examples available on the device. That is cheap, but it assumes the backbone already sees the deployment environment in the right way. When the environment changes the image appearance, the few labels must fight both the new task and the mismatch in visual features. Another beginner might fine-tune the whole backbone on the device once local examples arrive. That can adapt more directly, but it asks a limited device to run a heavy training job, and it may overreact to very few labeled examples. A third attempt would collect target-environment data in advance, but the abstract states that such samples are typically unavailable before deployment.
632.ap: Glasses makes a narrower move: use one unlabeled image from the deployment environment as a clue about the local visual world, then let the cloud do the heavy adaptation work and send back lightweight model updates for the device. The important point is that the image does not need a task label. It acts as an environmental fingerprint: not a statement that this is a cat or a defect, but evidence about lighting, texture, viewpoint, and scene style. The cloud supplies computation and sample resources that the device lacks. Instead of asking the edge device to retune the full visual backbone, Glasses produces updates meant to adapt the ViT-based backbone rapidly to the deployment environment. The result is still aimed at improving few-shot learning on the device, but the expensive part of preparing the adaptation is shifted away from the device and away from scarce labeled target examples.
632.mech: The input is a pretrained ViT-based visual backbone already intended for edge use, a deployment device, and one image from the environment where the device will operate. That image is unlabeled, so the mechanism cannot learn a new class from it directly. It can only read the environment's visual character. The device-cloud collaboration begins with the device providing that environment image or the information derived from it to the cloud. The cloud has two advantages named in the abstract: more computation and access to sample resources. It uses those resources to compute model updates that adapt the backbone toward the target environment. In plain terms, the cloud asks: how should the visual feature extractor be nudged so images from this setting are easier for later few-shot learning to use? The updates are designed to be lightweight, so the device receives a small adaptation package rather than running a full expensive training process. After this backbone adaptation, the device performs few-shot learning for downstream tasks using one or five labeled examples. The transformed object is therefore not mainly the single environment image; the transformed object is the model's internal visual processing. The output is an environment-adapted backbone on the edge device, which the abstract reports gives better few-shot performance than the original pretrained backbone across five models and two datasets.
632.math: The main mathematical idea is learning from examples under a strict budget. A visual model is a rule with many adjustable settings. Each setting affects how raw image pixels become intermediate visual evidence and then a task prediction. Ordinary fine-tuning defines what counts as wrong on labeled examples and changes settings to reduce that wrongness. Glasses cannot rely on many labeled environment examples, so the adaptation signal is different: one unlabeled environment image tells the system about the source of visual mismatch, while cloud-side samples and computation help turn that clue into usable updates. A second idea is controlled approximation, the efficiency family's core tradeoff. Instead of paying the full cost of tuning every part of a large backbone on the device, the method tries to change only what is needed for rapid adaptation. A third idea is representation alignment, meaning the model's internal descriptions of images should be moved so the deployment environment is not treated as an alien visual source. The ViT backbone adds a focusing mechanism: image pieces are combined with learned weights, so adaptation can change how visual pieces influence one another. The tradeoff is accuracy versus device cost, with another tradeoff between adapting enough to handle the new environment and changing so much that the broad pretrained knowledge is damaged.
632.dots: This paper connects most directly to the repo's Efficiency & Scalability family. That family is about preserving the decision signal while cutting waste; here the waste would be full device-side backbone tuning for every deployment environment. It also belongs near the Multimodal & Vision-Language family because the shared issue is visual adaptation under real deployment pressure, especially when large pretrained visual systems must become useful for local tasks with little data. The self-supervised thread is nearby as well: Glasses uses an unlabeled environment image, so the image provides a teaching signal without a human class label. Compared with retrieval or recommendation papers that save work by pruning candidates, this paper saves work by moving adaptation into a device-cloud split and sending only lightweight updates back. Compared with privacy or federated papers, it is less about hiding data and more about where computation and sample resources live. The common 2026 pressure is deployment-shaped learning: models must adjust after they leave the lab.
632.ww: The approach should help because environment mismatch can poison the few-shot stage before the few labels even start doing useful work. If the backbone already encodes the target environment in a friendlier way, then the one or five labeled examples can spend their limited evidence on the actual downstream distinction rather than correcting lighting, background, camera, or style mismatch. The cloud is useful because it can afford computations and sample comparisons that would be awkward on the device. The unlabeled environment image is useful because it arrives exactly from the place where the device will operate; even without a label, it can reveal the local appearance pattern that the pretrained model did not specialize for. The lightweight update is the bridge between those two facts. It lets the device benefit from cloud-side adaptation without carrying the cost of full training. The reported gains over the original backbone in one-shot and five-shot settings are consistent with this story: the adaptation improves the starting visual description before the scarce labeled examples are used.
632.po: The payoff is faster environment-aware few-shot learning on edge devices. According to the abstract, Glasses works with ViT-based backbones, uses only one unlabeled environment image, and relies on device-cloud collaboration to produce rapid model updates. In experiments with five models and two datasets, it outperforms the original backbone by 5.54 percent to 22.56 percent in the one-shot setting and by 2.50 percent to 10.28 percent in the five-shot setting. Practically, that buys a way to deploy pretrained visual models into new environments without waiting for a labeled target dataset or asking the device to perform heavy backbone tuning.
632.limits: The claim depends on one environment image carrying enough information about the deployment setting. That may fail if the environment is highly varied, if lighting changes sharply, or if the single image misses the conditions that matter later. The method also assumes a cloud connection or at least a path for cloud-generated updates, so it may not fit fully disconnected devices. The abstract reports results on five models and two datasets, but it does not prove coverage across all edge hardware, camera types, environments, tasks, or safety-critical uses. It also does not specify in the abstract what data the cloud samples come from, how privacy is handled, or which parts of the backbone are changed.

633.bp: Many web products now do more than display pages or return a fixed list of links. They choose music, articles, products, answers, summaries, and follow-up actions while a person is still forming a need. This keynote is about that shift: AI is becoming part of the experience itself, not only a hidden component behind it. The ordinary-world problem is a platform such as Spotify trying to help people search, receive recommendations, talk to an interface, explore unfamiliar content, and still feel in control. The hard object is the user's intent, because it is often partial, changing, and expressed through clicks, queries, skips, conversations, and exploration. The paper serves builders of web systems who must design search, recommendation, conversational, and generative interfaces together at web scale. Its contribution is not a single new algorithm, but a map of design choices, deployment pressures, and research questions for AI-driven web experiences.
633.wh: The difficulty comes from joining three things that pull against each other. First, users want the system to understand intent even when they do not state it cleanly. Second, the platform must choose from a huge and constantly changing body of content. Third, the experience has to remain interactive and controllable, so the user can steer rather than simply accept a machine's guess. A simple search box or recommendation list treats the user need as already known. But in exploration and discovery, the need is often discovered through the interaction itself. Conversational and generative interfaces add another layer: the system may produce text or suggestions, not only retrieve existing items, so mistakes can be more visible and harder to audit. At scale, deployment is also part of the problem. A method that works in a demo must handle many users, fast responses, changing content, product constraints, and open questions about how future web interactions should be designed.
633.naive: A smart beginner would build separate systems: one search engine that matches query words to content, one recommender that repeats items similar to past clicks or listens, and one conversational interface that answers user messages. That separation feels clean because each tool has a clear job. It fails because the user's experience is not separated. A search may become a recommendation moment; a recommendation may invite a conversation; a conversation may reveal a new intent that should change future rankings. The beginner might also optimize for immediate clicks or plays, but exploration and discovery require exposing useful unknowns, not only repeating the familiar. Finally, a black-box automated experience can remove user control, which conflicts with the abstract's emphasis on intent-aware and user-controllable systems.
633.ap: The central move is to treat web experience design as an interactive loop between user intent, AI models, and system infrastructure. Instead of viewing AI as a back-end scoring module, the keynote frames it as something that shapes what the user can ask, see, refine, and generate. In concrete terms, search and recommendation become less like one-shot lookups and more like guided conversations with a large content service. The system observes signals from the current session and past behavior, estimates what the user may be trying to do, offers ranked or generated choices, and gives the user ways to steer the next step. Recent AI methods matter here because they can learn from many examples and produce flexible outputs, while web-system design matters because those outputs must be delivered reliably at scale. The core idea is therefore not automation alone, but automation with interaction, intent awareness, deployment discipline, and user control.
633.mech: The mechanism, as supported by the abstract, is a design pattern rather than a fully specified algorithm. The inputs are web-scale content, user actions, search requests, recommendation histories, conversational turns, and product constraints from a deployed service context such as Spotify. First, the system gathers signs of intent: what the user asked for, what they selected, what they skipped, what context they are in, and possibly what they say in a conversational interface. Second, learned models turn those signs into internal descriptions of both the user need and the available content. This is a compression step: rich behavior and content are reduced to comparable signals that a system can score. Third, search and recommendation components compare the current need with candidate content and rank a small set of possible next items or actions. Fourth, generative components, meaning models that create new text or interface responses rather than only selecting stored items, may turn those candidates into conversational or exploratory experiences. Fifth, the interface exposes controls so the user can redirect the system, making the next round of evidence better. The output is not just a ranked list; it is an evolving interaction in which retrieval, recommendation, generation, and user feedback continually reshape one another.
633.math: The abstract names deep learning and generative models, so the mathematical story should be stated carefully. Deep learning means learning many layers of adjustable rules from examples, where early layers capture simple signals and later layers combine them into more task-specific judgments. In this setting, those judgments may concern what content matches a query, what a user may want next, or what response would support exploration. Ranking is another central idea: when a platform has far more possible items than it can show, it gives candidates scores and orders them so the most useful few appear first. Similarity also matters: the system must decide when two songs, queries, sessions, or expressed intents are close enough to inform each other, while recognizing that closeness compresses away detail. Probability is implicit because user intent is uncertain; the system is estimating chances from partial evidence rather than reading a user's mind. Optimization, in plain language, is defining what counts as a bad experience, such as irrelevant results, weak discovery, poor control, or slow response, then adjusting model and system choices to reduce that badness. The tradeoff is personalization versus control, flexibility versus reliability, and richer interaction versus deployment cost.
633.dots: This keynote sits at the meeting point of several recurring conference ideas. It connects to information retrieval because search is still about choosing useful evidence from a huge collection, but the query may now be conversational and evolving. It connects to recommender systems because platforms such as Spotify must pick a small set of content for a particular person and moment, while avoiding the trap of only repeating what already looked popular or familiar. It connects to language models because generative interfaces can produce responses and explanations, not just rank stored objects. It also connects to efficiency and scalability because all of this has to run for many users under real latency, infrastructure, and deployment constraints. The broader field question is how web systems should change when AI is no longer a replaceable ranking box. The same pressure appears across search, recommendation, retrieval-augmented answers, personalization, and human-in-the-loop systems: infer intent, choose well, explain or generate usefully, and let the user correct the course.
633.ww: The approach should work better than the naive setup because it treats intent as something revealed over time. A fixed search engine asks the user to express the need perfectly at the start. A fixed recommender assumes past behavior is enough. An interactive, intent-aware system can use each action as new evidence. If the user refines a request, skips a suggestion, follows a surprising recommendation, or asks a conversational follow-up, the system can change what it compares and ranks next. Learned models help because they can reuse patterns across many users and content items without requiring engineers to hand-write every rule. Generative interfaces can help because they turn selection into dialogue: the system can present options, ask or answer follow-up questions, and support exploration when the user does not know the exact target. User control is crucial to the logic. Without it, personalization can become a closed loop where the system confidently narrows the world. With steering, the user's corrections become part of the evidence stream, making discovery more deliberate.
633.po: The payoff is a clearer design direction for web experiences where search, recommendation, conversation, and generation are not isolated products. Grounded in Spotify-style deployed systems, the keynote points toward interfaces that are more interactive, more aware of user intent, and more supportive of exploration and discovery. For users, that means a system can help them move from a vague need to useful content without requiring perfect query wording. For builders, it highlights the system patterns and deployment challenges that must be handled before such experiences can work at web scale. The practical gain is not a reported accuracy number; it is a framework for thinking about future web interaction design.
633.limits: Because this is a keynote abstract, it does not prove a particular model, training method, metric, or deployment architecture. It says the talk draws on Spotify experience and discusses emerging system patterns, deployment challenges, and open research questions, but it does not give experimental details in the input file. The claims therefore depend on the assumption that lessons from one large content platform transfer to other web systems with different users, content, incentives, and safety needs. Intent-aware personalization must also avoid over-narrowing choices, misreading user signals, or hiding too much control. Generative interfaces add risks around reliability and user trust. The abstract motivates these issues; it does not settle them.

634.bp: The ordinary problem is deciding whether a group of language-model agents can stand in for a real human group when people are trying to solve a difficult social question. A useful social simulation is not just several agents talking at once. It must show when participants share knowledge, when they challenge one another, when they trust a more capable peer, and when they resist a weak or biased argument. This matters for web-scale social questions because platforms, courts, medical teams, and online communities often need decision support before an intervention is tried in the real world. BEACOF starts from the fact that human collaboration changes while the conversation unfolds. A person may begin cooperatively, become skeptical after a poor answer, or defer after seeing expertise. The paper proposes agents that maintain beliefs about peer capabilities and use those beliefs to choose a collaboration style instead of being locked into one fixed pattern.
634.wh: The hard part is that a group's interaction pattern and its knowledge about members are tangled together. To know whether an agent should cooperate, debate, or critique, it needs some estimate of what the other agents can contribute. But that estimate is learned through the very interaction pattern being chosen. If the topology is fixed, the system avoids this circular problem by pretending it does not exist: the same agents speak to the same neighbors in the same way. That is easier to engineer, but it misses the swing between knowledge sharing and critical disagreement that the abstract says appears in real scenarios. Too much agreement creates groupthink, where weak ideas become accepted because nobody challenges them. Too much opposition creates deadlock, where agents spend effort blocking one another rather than improving the answer. A credible simulation must keep both forces available and decide when each is useful under incomplete information.
634.naive: A smart beginner would make a fixed multi-agent recipe. For example, every agent might first propose an answer, then every other agent critiques it, then a final agent combines the responses. Or the designer might hard-code a team graph where some agents always cooperate and others always debate. This can look organized, but it assumes the best social structure is known before the conversation begins. It fails when the needed structure depends on hidden capability. A medical scenario may need deference to a strong specialist; a judicial scenario may need adversarial testing; an open social discussion may need synthesis. A fixed recipe cannot notice that one peer is becoming more trustworthy or that a debate has become unproductive.
634.ap: The core move is to make collaboration itself an adaptive decision. BEACOF treats each agent as uncertain about the other agents' capabilities. Instead of assuming that everyone knows who is good at what, each agent carries a probability-like belief: based on what I have seen so far, how likely is this peer to be useful for this part of the problem? The agent then chooses a collaboration type according to that belief and the current state of the discussion. The paper draws this from Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium, a game-theory idea for situations where players act over time while holding incomplete knowledge about one another. In plain terms, each agent keeps updating its picture of the room and chooses a move that makes sense given that picture. The system is approximate because full exact equilibrium reasoning would be too heavy for realistic language-agent simulations.
634.mech: The mechanism begins with a social-simulation task, such as the adversarial judicial, open-ended social, or mixed medical settings named in the abstract. Several language-model agents enter the task, but they do not simply follow a static interaction graph. Each agent starts with limited information about the capabilities of the others. As the conversation proceeds, the agents observe peer contributions: who gives useful evidence, who catches mistakes, who helps combine partial ideas, and who pushes disagreement without progress. Those observations are converted into changing beliefs about capability. The next collaboration choice is then made from two ingredients: the agent's current belief about its peers and the current need of the group. If the group needs knowledge synthesis, an agent can move toward cooperation. If an answer needs stress testing, it can move toward competitive critical reasoning. If a peer appears more capable on the present issue, the agent can give that peer more influence; if a peer appears unreliable, it can reduce reliance or challenge more. This loop repeats, so behavior at one step becomes evidence for later steps. The output is not only a final answer, but a more lifelike path of interaction that avoids both false consensus and stalled conflict.
634.math: The main mathematical idea is a dynamic game with incomplete information. A game here does not mean entertainment; it means several decision makers whose best moves depend on what the others may do. Dynamic means the interaction has a sequence: what happens now changes what should happen next. Incomplete information means an agent does not directly know another agent's capability, so it must estimate it from observed behavior. Probability supplies the language for these estimates. A belief is a disciplined way to say, "given the evidence so far, this peer seems more or less capable," while still admitting uncertainty. Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium adds a consistency requirement: each participant should choose a sensible action given its current beliefs, and those beliefs should be updated from the observed history rather than held fixed. BEACOF uses an approximate version of this idea, which matters because exact reasoning over every possible belief and future conversation path would likely be impractical. The tradeoff is realism versus cost. Richer belief tracking can model human-like adaptation, but it depends on whether the observed agent outputs are reliable evidence of capability.
634.dots: This paper sits in the repo's LLM agents and tool-use family because it asks how a language model becomes a participant in a controlled workflow rather than a single answer generator. It is close to multi-agent workflow papers that split work across roles, but it addresses a failure noted across the family: adding agents does not automatically add reliability if their coordination is poor. It also connects to social networks and influence, because the useful signal is not stored inside one agent; it moves through relations, replies, trust, and disagreement over time. The probability concept is central because agents act before they know exactly who is competent. The controlled-choice idea is also present: each agent repeatedly chooses a collaboration mode under constraints. Nearby repo themes include PolicySim-style social simulation, agent group chat, multi-agent misinformation detection, and cognitive world modeling, all of which depend on believable social behavior rather than fluent text alone.
634.ww: BEACOF should improve over a fixed topology because it makes the source of coordination failure visible to the system. Groupthink happens when agreement is treated as safety even though agreement may only reflect social pressure or repeated weak reasoning. Deadlock happens when criticism continues even after it stops producing better evidence. Belief updates give the agents a middle path. If one agent repeatedly contributes useful structure, the others have a reason to rely on it more. If an agent's challenges expose errors, debate remains valuable. If challenges stop helping, the system can shift back toward synthesis. This is the intuitive force behind the game-theory framing: a good move is not chosen in isolation, but in response to what the agent currently believes about the others and what the group needs next. The abstract's claim that BEACOF prevents coordination failures and converges toward higher-quality solutions follows from this adaptive loop, at least in the tested judicial, social, and medical settings.
634.po: The payoff is a more credible social simulation for decision-support settings where the pattern of interaction matters as much as the final answer. The abstract reports validation across adversarial judicial scenarios, open-ended social scenarios, and mixed medical scenarios. In practical terms, BEACOF buys a way for agents to shift between cooperation and critique instead of being trapped in one designer-chosen graph. That can make simulated groups less prone to shallow agreement and less likely to stall in unproductive conflict. The result is useful for builders who need agent societies that behave more like changing human groups.
634.limits: The abstract does not provide the exact belief-update rule, the approximation method, the evaluation metrics, or the datasets, so those details cannot be verified from the input. The method assumes that an agent's visible contributions are meaningful evidence of its capability; if language models sound confident while being wrong, beliefs can update in the wrong direction. It also assumes that the chosen collaboration types cover the important human interaction modes in judicial, social, and medical settings. Validation across three scenario types is encouraging, but it does not prove reliable behavior for every culture, institution, task difficulty, model family, or adversarial participant.

635.bp: DMAP serves a common but difficult reading task: a person asks a question about a complex document, and the system must find the answer from text, figures, tables, charts, layout, and references between parts. A human reader does not treat a document as a bag of sentences. The reader notices that a paragraph belongs under a section heading, that a chart may explain a number mentioned nearby, and that a cross-reference points to another part of the argument. Existing multimodal document question-answering systems often flatten this rich object into separate text chunks, then search for chunks that sound similar to the question. DMAP starts from the opposite view. The document itself has a shape, and that shape carries meaning. The paper builds a document-level map that keeps the hierarchy and relationships visible, so answering becomes guided reading rather than loose text matching.
635.wh: The hard part is that document evidence is not only in words. It is also in placement, nesting, labels, captions, tables, figures, and cross-references. A paragraph can mean something different because it appears under a particular section. A figure may answer a question only when paired with nearby explanation. A table cell may matter because of its row label, column label, and the section that introduced it. Flat retrieval breaks these dependencies by cutting the document into disconnected pieces and asking which piece looks semantically close to the question. That can retrieve a locally relevant sentence while losing the reason it matters. The central tension is therefore speed and simplicity versus faithful context. A system wants a small amount of evidence, because reading the whole document every time is wasteful, but the evidence cannot be chosen as if the document had no structure.
635.naive: A smart beginner would split the document into chunks, turn each chunk into a searchable representation, retrieve the chunks whose wording is closest to the question, and ask a language model to answer from them. This is appealing because it is simple and works well when the answer is contained in one paragraph. It fails when the answer depends on relationships: a figure and its caption, a section and its subsections, a table and the text that interprets it, or a reference from one page to another. The beginner system may find words that match the question but miss the structural path a human would follow. It treats neighboring, nested, and cited evidence as accidental rather than meaningful.
635.ap: The core idea is to give the document an explicit internal map before trying to answer questions. DMAP, the document map, organizes text together with figures, tables, charts, and other visual elements into a hierarchy that resembles how people read: broad sections contain narrower parts, and related visual and textual elements are connected. The paper uses a Structured-Semantic Understanding Agent, meaning an automated builder that reads the document elements and arranges them into this schema while preserving both content meaning and page layout. A second component, the Reflective Reasoning Agent, uses the map during answering. It does not only retrieve once and stop. It checks whether the gathered context is enough, then returns to the map for targeted evidence when the answer still lacks support. The main move is replacing one-shot flat search with structure-aware, evidence-driven navigation.
635.mech: The mechanism begins with a multimodal document: text blocks, section organization, figures, tables, charts, and layout relations on the page. First, the Structured-Semantic Understanding Agent identifies the document elements and organizes them into a human-aligned hierarchy. In plain terms, it decides which pieces belong inside larger pieces, such as which content belongs to a section, and it records relationships between elements, such as figure-text correspondence and cross-reference links. The output of this stage is DMAP, a document-specific map rather than a generic pile of chunks. When a question arrives, the system searches this map for relevant evidence. Because the map contains hierarchy and links, retrieval can follow document structure: from a section to its children, from a textual mention to a figure, or from a cross-reference to the cited part. The Reflective Reasoning Agent then tries to answer from the retrieved context. It also judges whether the current evidence is sufficient. If the evidence is thin, mismatched, or incomplete, it asks the map for more targeted context instead of guessing from the first retrieved pieces. The final output is an answer grounded in evidence selected through both meaning and structure.
635.math: The main mathematical object is a structured map. Its places are document elements: sections, text blocks, figures, tables, charts, captions, and referenced parts. Its links say how those elements relate: one element contains another, appears near another, explains another, or points to another. This is graph reasoning in everyday language: when two pieces are connected for a real document reason, evidence can travel between them. A figure is not just similar to nearby text; the document layout says they may jointly explain something. A second idea is ranking, which means choosing a useful order from many possible evidence pieces. The system must decide which parts of the map should be read first for a question. A third idea is similarity, but not only word similarity. Closeness now includes structural closeness: being in the same section, linked by a reference, or paired across figure and text. The tradeoff is local match versus global coherence. A chunk may match the question's words but sit in the wrong part of the document. A structurally connected piece may use different words yet be necessary for the answer. DMAP's math fits because documents are not independent records; they are organized objects whose links carry evidence.
635.dots: This paper connects to three recurring repo themes. Like information retrieval and search papers, it asks how to choose a small useful set from a much larger collection, because the answer system cannot read everything with equal care. Like network and graph papers, it treats relationships as evidence: a link between a paragraph and a figure is a reason to move attention from one to the other. Like multimodal vision-language work, it must align unlike signals, especially written text, visual elements, and page layout. It also sits near retrieval-augmented generation, where an answer model is supplied with outside evidence before writing. DMAP's difference is that the outside evidence is not retrieved from a flat store. It is retrieved from a document map whose structure mirrors human interpretive patterns. The neighboring idea is simple: better answering often starts before generation, at the point where evidence is represented, filtered, and checked.
635.ww: DMAP should improve over the naive approach because it preserves the clues that make document reading reliable. A flat chunk system must infer context after it has already cut that context apart. DMAP keeps context available as part of the search surface. If a question points toward a section, the system can inspect related subsections. If a text mention depends on a figure or table, the map gives the system a path to that evidence. If a first retrieval is not enough, the reasoning component can ask for another targeted interaction with the map instead of treating the first results as final. This matters because document questions often require a chain of support rather than a single sentence. The abstract's reported gains in retrieval precision and reasoning consistency follow from this mechanism: retrieval becomes less likely to gather isolated but misleading snippets, and reasoning becomes less likely to mix pieces that do not belong together. The method works by making the document's own organization constrain the answer process.
635.po: The payoff is a document question-answering system that can handle multimodal documents more like a careful reader. According to the local full record, experiments on MMDocQA benchmarks show that DMAP creates document-specific structural representations aligned with human interpretive patterns. The reported practical gains are higher retrieval precision, more consistent reasoning, and stronger multimodal comprehension than conventional retrieval-augmented generation approaches that rely on flatter evidence stores. In ordinary terms, the system is meant to find the right supporting parts of a complex document more reliably before it answers.
635.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The system must correctly detect document elements and their relationships; a bad map can guide reasoning toward the wrong place. The document's layout and references must actually reflect meaning, which is usually true for well-formed reports but less reliable for noisy scans, unusual templates, or badly converted files. The sufficiency check must recognize when evidence is incomplete rather than becoming falsely confident. The abstract reports benchmark improvements, but it does not prove that DMAP handles every document genre, language, scan quality, table design, or adversarially confusing layout. It also does not specify from the abstract alone how costly map construction is for very large collections.

636.bp: This paper is about a daily platform decision that becomes difficult at LinkedIn scale: which personalized email, recommendation, or action should be served to a particular member right now. The system is not choosing for one person in isolation. It is serving many users, many business objectives, and several stakeholders whose goals may conflict. One email may help a member discover a job, another may support a business campaign, and a third may protect attention by not overusing a channel. The abstract frames BanditLP as a production method for this kind of repeated choice. It combines learning what each action is likely to produce with a serving-time allocation step that respects constraints. The need appears before the method: a large platform must keep learning from feedback while still honoring budgets, policies, and stakeholder limits when real users are waiting for decisions.
636.wh: The hard part is that the system must learn and obey rules at the same time. If it only learns from past outcomes, it may keep showing actions that already looked good and never gather evidence about uncertain alternatives. If it only explores uncertain actions, it can waste user attention and business capacity. If it only applies fixed constraints, it may satisfy rules while missing the actions most likely to help each specific user. Multi-stakeholder recommendation adds another tension: the best action for one objective may crowd out another objective, and the best-looking action for one user may consume capacity that could have produced more value elsewhere. The abstract also stresses web scale, including an LP solver handling billions of variables. That means the difficulty is not only statistical. The decision space is enormous, and the answer must be produced at serving time rather than after a slow offline study.
636.naive: A smart beginner might train a prediction model for each possible email outcome, score every candidate action for the current user, and send the action with the highest predicted score. That simple plan fails in three ways. First, it trusts what is already known and may stop testing actions whose value is uncertain. Second, it treats the highest local score as enough, even when the platform has delivery limits, campaign goals, fairness requirements, or other stakeholder constraints. Third, it does not scale gracefully when millions of users and actions create an enormous grid of possible choices. Another beginner might write hand rules for those constraints, but hand rules become brittle when objectives change and when the learned response estimates move over time.
636.ap: BanditLP's core idea is to split the work into two coordinated jobs. The first job learns uncertain outcome estimates for each objective-specific action. The abstract says this uses neural Thompson Sampling, meaning a learned predictor represents what may happen for a user-action pair and deliberately leaves room for uncertainty-driven trials. The second job chooses actions through a large linear program, which is a table of decision variables, scores, and constraints used to find the best allowed allocation. In concrete terms, the learner says, for this context and this candidate action, here is a plausible value for each objective. The solver then asks, across all active serving decisions, which choices give high value while still satisfying the platform's limits. The central move is not just better prediction. It is integrating exploration with constrained action selection in the same production loop.
636.mech: The mechanism starts with a serving opportunity: a user context and a set of candidate recommendation actions, such as possible email marketing choices in the LinkedIn application mentioned by the abstract. First, neural outcome models read the context and action descriptions and estimate objective-specific outcomes. The abstract does not list those objectives, so they should be understood generally as measurable results the system cares about. Second, Thompson Sampling turns uncertainty into controlled randomness. Instead of using only one fixed best estimate, the system samples from its current belief about possible outcomes. Actions with strong evidence are usually valued consistently; actions with little evidence can occasionally look promising enough to be tried, which creates future feedback. Third, those sampled or predicted values become coefficients in a large linear program. The linear program contains variables representing possible action selections and constraints representing business, stakeholder, or serving limits. Fourth, the LP solver searches over the huge set of allowed assignments, reportedly at a scale of billions of variables. It selects actions that score well under the learned objective values while remaining feasible under constraints. Finally, the system serves the chosen action, observes feedback, and that feedback can improve later outcome estimates. The output is therefore a production policy: a rule that learns from interaction while making constrained recommendations at serving time.
636.math: The first mathematical idea is a contextual bandit. In plain language, the system sees a situation, chooses one action, and later observes feedback for that chosen action, not for every action it could have chosen. The context is the information available about the user and serving moment; the action is the recommendation or email choice; the reward is the measured outcome. The second idea is Thompson Sampling. It treats each action's value as uncertain, draws a plausible value from the current belief, and chooses using that draw. This makes exploration natural: an uncertain action is tested only when the evidence still leaves a real chance that it may be best. The third idea is a neural predictor, meaning a flexible learned function that can map rich user and action information to outcome estimates. The fourth idea is linear programming. A linear program defines decision variables, adds weighted values, and imposes constraints as straight-line accounting rules: do not exceed a budget, satisfy a quota, or keep an allocation within allowed limits. The tradeoff is exploration versus exploitation, plus reward versus feasibility. BanditLP matters because probability handles uncertainty about outcomes, while constrained optimization handles the platform's need to choose only actions that are allowed.
636.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of recommendation, probability, ranking, and constrained allocation. It connects to the recommender-systems family because it chooses a small useful action from a large changing pile, but it treats selection as a live decision rather than only an offline ranking problem. It connects to the reinforcement-learning family because present actions produce the feedback that shapes future choices. It also neighbors the off-policy evaluation paper in the same batch, which questions how reliably contextual bandit policies can be judged from logged data when assumptions about the logs fail. Another nearby sibling in the repo is the limited-supply contextual bandit work, where recommendation quality must be balanced against scarce inventory. BanditLP has a similar deeper shape, but its abstract emphasizes multi-stakeholder constraints and production serving. The broader conference idea is that web systems increasingly need learned choice plus explicit limits, not one without the other.
636.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it gives each source of difficulty its own machinery. Uncertain learning is handled by Thompson Sampling: when evidence is thin, the system does not pretend to know the answer; it sometimes tests plausible alternatives and uses the resulting feedback. Rich user and action descriptions are handled by neural outcome models, which can reuse patterns across many examples instead of requiring a separate counter for every user-action pair. Feasibility is handled by the linear program: the final served action is not merely the highest local score, but part of an allocation that satisfies constraints. This matters in multi-stakeholder settings because constraints are not incidental details. They are part of what makes an action acceptable. The abstract's claim of consistent gains over strong baselines and a LinkedIn email marketing business win is plausible under this design because the system can learn better outcome estimates while preventing the serving layer from violating operational rules. The gain comes from coupling adaptive evidence gathering with disciplined allocation.
636.po: The payoff is a recommendation system that can operate in a realistic production setting where learning, personalization, and constraints all matter at once. The abstract says BanditLP is application-agnostic, compatible with arbitrary neural architectures, and deployable at web scale. Its LP solver is described as capable of handling billions of variables, which is the practical bridge from a clean mathematical idea to a serving system. Experiments on public benchmarks and synthetic data show consistent gains over strong baselines, and the LinkedIn email marketing application reports a business win. The concrete capability is not just sending better emails; it is making constrained personalized decisions while continuing to explore what works.
636.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The observed feedback must be a meaningful measure of the objectives; if email clicks or business outcomes miss user fatigue or long-term trust, the system may optimize the wrong thing. Thompson Sampling depends on uncertainty estimates that are not badly overconfident. The linear program depends on constraints that correctly encode stakeholder needs, and it can only protect goals that are written into the model. The abstract reports benchmarks, synthetic data, and one LinkedIn application, but it does not prove the same behavior across every recommendation domain. It also does not specify the objectives, constraints, failure cases, or how delayed and biased feedback are handled.

637.bp: This keynote is about the next missing layer in AI systems that live around people. A chat system, image system, or digital assistant can already recognize patterns, generate text, and act across web platforms. But when it is placed inside a school, workplace, hospital, marketplace, or public institution, the useful question is no longer just "what answer fits this input?" The system has to understand the situation people believe they are in, what they are trying to accomplish, what actions may change later events, and what social rules make an action acceptable or harmful. The paper calls this Cognitive World Modeling: a persistent picture of reality that joins the physical world, such as time, space, cause, and action, with the mental world, such as goals, beliefs, intentions, emotions, and norms. The real aim is AI that can collaborate over time, not merely react once.
637.wh: The difficulty is that human life is not just a stream of visible events. Two people can do the same action for different reasons; the same words can be helpful in one setting and offensive in another; the same recommendation can be safe for one person and risky for another because of hidden goals or beliefs. A system that only predicts the next likely answer may learn regularities in language and images without knowing what those regularities mean to a person who must live with the consequence. The abstract argues that collaboration requires a durable model, not a momentary response. The system must keep track of what happened before, what changed because of an action, what each person may believe, and which social expectations constrain the next move. That is hard because physical facts and mental states interact: a delayed train, a false belief, and a social obligation can jointly determine what someone should do.
637.naive: A smart beginner might try to solve this by adding more instructions to a language model: be helpful, consider context, avoid harm, explain your answer, and follow social norms. That can improve surface behavior, but it leaves the system guessing from text patterns at the moment of response. It does not necessarily maintain a stable picture of what is true, what changed over time, what action caused what outcome, or what another person believes and wants. Another simple attempt is to bolt on safety checks after an answer is produced. The abstract rejects that as too late: trust and alignment should come from the system's internal model of people and consequences, not from a filter attached after reasoning has already gone wrong.
637.ap: The central move is to treat understanding as world modeling in two joined layers. The first layer is physical: events unfold in time, objects and people occupy places, actions change later states, and causes connect what someone does to what happens next. The second layer is mental and social: people have goals, partial beliefs, intentions, emotions, and norms that shape what actions mean. Cognitive World Modeling asks the AI to maintain one evolving representation that holds both layers together. Instead of answering only from the immediate prompt, the system would ask: what is the current situation, what do the people involved believe, what are they trying to do, what actions are available, what consequences might follow, and which consequences matter to humans? In that framing, explanation, planning, adaptation, collaboration, alignment, and trust are not separate add-ons. They are behaviors that become possible when the model tracks reality as people experience it.
637.mech: The abstract is a keynote proposal, so it does not specify an implemented algorithm. But its mechanism can be read as a pipeline of information the system would need to maintain. First, observations enter from language, images, digital actions, and the surrounding platform. Second, the system places those observations into a persistent state rather than treating each exchange as isolated: what happened, when it happened, who was involved, and what physical or institutional constraints apply. Third, it builds links between actions and possible consequences, so a proposed step is not just scored as plausible but considered as something that may change the future. Fourth, it represents people inside the scene as agents with beliefs, goals, intentions, emotions, and social expectations. This matters because a response that ignores a user's belief or obligation may be factually correct but practically wrong. Fifth, when planning or explaining, the system compares possible actions by their likely physical outcomes and by their human meaning. The output is therefore not merely a generated answer. It is an action, plan, explanation, or adaptation grounded in a continuing model of the external world and the humans within it. The key transformation is from one-shot pattern response to maintained, consequence-aware context.
637.math: The main mathematical ideas are representation, causality, sequential state, and belief modeling. A representation is a compressed map: it cannot contain every detail of the world, so it must decide which facts to keep because they help future reasoning. Here the kept facts are not only objects and events but also human goals, beliefs, emotions, and norms. Causality means asking what would change if an action changed, instead of merely noticing that two things often appear together. That fits the paper because collaboration depends on consequences: a system should understand what its advice may cause. Sequential state means that time matters; the current situation is partly defined by earlier events and by commitments that persist. Belief modeling means keeping separate what is true from what a person thinks is true. This is essential because people act from their beliefs, even when those beliefs are incomplete or mistaken. The tradeoff is compression versus meaning: a model must simplify the world enough to reason, but if it drops the wrong human detail, such as a norm or intention, it may produce an answer that is technically fluent and socially misaligned.
637.dots: Within the repo's conference map, this paper sits near LLM Agents & Tool Use, Explainability & Interpretability, Causal Inference, Time Series & Spatiotemporal reasoning, Knowledge Graphs, Multimodal & Vision-Language systems, and Recommender Systems. The connection is not that all these papers use the same method. It is that many are trying to make AI decisions less isolated. DMAP keeps document structure so an answer is grounded in where evidence appears. BEACOF models agents that update beliefs about one another during collaboration. Time-TK treats time as structure rather than a flat list of observations. DHHGN uses evolving relations in a knowledge graph to forecast future facts. BanditLP treats recommendation as action under uncertainty and constraints. This keynote names the broader pressure behind those efforts: web AI is moving from classifying or ranking static inputs toward acting with memory, context, consequence, and human meaning.
637.ww: The idea should work when errors come from missing situation structure rather than from lack of surface fluency. A system that tracks only words may answer in a way that sounds reasonable while ignoring a user's goal, a prior commitment, or a downstream consequence. A system with a physical-and-mental world model has more places to catch that mistake. It can notice that an action changes a later state, that a person's belief differs from the facts, or that a social norm changes what counts as an acceptable response. This gives planning a better target: not just produce the most likely text, but choose an action whose expected consequences fit the human situation. It also makes explanations more natural. Instead of saying only what answer it selected, the system can point to the modeled chain: what it believed was happening, which human goal it was serving, what consequence it expected, and which norm or constraint shaped the choice.
637.po: The payoff is a research direction for AI systems that plan, explain, adapt, and collaborate over time. The abstract's practical claim is that trust and alignment become more natural when the system maintains an accurate, evolving model of both the outside world and the humans inside it. That would make AI more useful in settings where meaning matters: decision support, institutions, everyday assistance, and long-running collaboration. The paper does not promise a benchmark gain. Its contribution is a conceptual architecture for moving from reactive systems toward systems that reason about context and consequence.
637.limits: Because this is a talk abstract, many details remain open. It does not specify how to build the persistent representation, how to measure whether the mental model is accurate, how to update beliefs without invading privacy, or how to resolve conflicts between different people's goals and norms. The approach assumes that physical events, human beliefs, emotions, intentions, and social norms can be represented well enough to guide action. That may fail in unfamiliar cultures, ambiguous situations, adversarial settings, or cases where people themselves cannot state their goals clearly. The abstract also does not prove that alignment emerges automatically; it argues that better world models make trust more plausible.

638.bp: Modern web services live or fail by forecasts. A transportation service wants to know whether road demand will rise soon. A website operator wants to know whether throughput will spike before servers become overloaded. A trading or monitoring system wants the next stretch of measurements early enough to allocate resources, warn users, or avoid waste. The object being predicted is not a single isolated number; it is a stream of readings where the order of the readings matters. Time-TK serves this ordinary need: use the past shape of a time series to guess its future values. The paper's starting point is that many forecasting systems borrow a habit from language models: they turn each time step into an independent computational item, called a token. That is convenient, but web data often has repeated rhythms and cross-time relationships. The paper argues that the first representation of the sequence should preserve those relationships instead of forcing the later model to rediscover them.
638.wh: The hard part is that a long time series carries relationships at many distances at once. The current traffic reading may depend on the immediately previous reading, the same hour yesterday, and a recurring weekly pattern. Website throughput can have short bursts, daily cycles, and longer regularities. If each time step is converted separately, the model receives a pile of individually described moments, but the act of separating them can weaken the very evidence that forecasting needs: how one moment moves with another moment at a particular offset. The abstract calls this multi-offset temporal correlation, meaning fine-grained dependence between values that are separated by different time gaps. Long sequences make the problem sharper because there are more possible offsets and more chances to compress away useful structure. A forecasting method must therefore balance two pressures: keep enough cross-time detail to predict well, while keeping the representation concise enough to run inside existing models.
638.naive: A smart beginner might take the standard recipe used in many sequence models. First, split the time series into time steps. Second, turn each step into its own numeric description.
