Third, pass the resulting list to a powerful forecasting model and let it learn which earlier steps matter. This seems reasonable because the model can still see the order of the list. The failure is that the earliest conversion has already treated each moment as if it can be described alone. Relationships such as every seventh step moving together, or one offset carrying a delayed response from another, are not stored directly. The later model may infer some of them, but it is working after an information bottleneck has already thrown away or blurred part of the pattern.
638.ap: Time-TK's core move is to change the first description of the sequence. Instead of giving every time step an isolated numeric fingerprint, it builds a Multi-Offset Time Embedding, or MOTE, where embedding means a compact numeric description and multi-offset means it deliberately records relationships across several time gaps. The paper says it gives an upper bound on how well ordinary token-style descriptions can approximately reconstruct the original sequence, and uses that bound to guide the design. After MOTE, the paper builds Time-TK, a forecasting architecture that combines two components. Multi-Offset Interactive KAN, or MI-KAN, learns specific temporal patterns among offset sub-sequences. Multi-Offset Temporal Interaction, or MOTI, then captures dependencies between those sub-sequences so information from several offsets can be integrated globally. The central idea is not merely to make the model larger, but to make the input preserve the time structure that regular web data naturally contains.
638.mech: The mechanism begins with a time series: a measured sequence such as traffic flow, website throughput, or BTC/USDT throughput over time. A standard model would map each time point separately into a compact numeric form. Time-TK instead forms descriptions that are aware of several offsets. Conceptually, it looks at sub-sequences separated by different time gaps, because the useful question is not only what happened at time t, but how time t relates to time t minus one, time t minus several, and other regular positions in the sequence. MOTE produces a representation meant to reduce the loss caused by independent token descriptions. That representation can be plugged into existing forecasting models, according to the abstract, so it acts as a reusable front end. In the full Time-TK architecture, MI-KAN then learns patterns within multiple offset sub-sequences. KAN refers to Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, a function-learning model; here the important point is that it is used to represent temporal patterns rather than hand-code them. MOTI then lets those offset-specific parts interact, so the forecast is not made from separate offset clues in isolation. The model integrates local offset patterns into a global view of the long sequence and outputs future values. Training is judged by forecast error on real-world datasets.
638.math: The main mathematical object is an ordered sequence of numbers plus relationships between positions in that order. Correlation means two parts of the sequence tend to move together in a repeatable way; multi-offset correlation means this togetherness is checked across several time gaps, not only adjacent steps. The paper also uses reconstruction as a measuring idea: if a compact description cannot recover the important shape of the original sequence, then it has lost information before forecasting even begins. An upper bound is a ceiling on how good that recovery can be under a certain representation; the abstract says this bound exposes a limit of independent token-style descriptions and guides MOTE. Function learning is the next idea. A model is given examples of past sequences and future values, then adjusts its internal numeric rules to reduce forecast error. The Transformer part supplies machinery for comparing positions in a sequence, while the KAN part supplies another way to learn nonlinear functions, meaning rules where changes in input do not produce simple straight-line changes in output. The tradeoff is compression versus detail: MOTE must keep offset structure without carrying every raw point in an expensive form.
638.dots: This paper sits in the time-series and spatiotemporal family because it treats the past as structured evidence for the future. It is close to other forecasting papers in the repo that ask how to preserve order, rhythm, and dependency under resource limits. The sequence concept connects directly: Time-TK refuses to treat the record as a flat pile, because a reading's meaning depends on where it falls in the ordered stream. It also touches the information concept, since the paper frames standard token descriptions as a bottleneck that loses reconstructive detail. It connects to similarity through correlation: the system must decide which shifted parts of a sequence are alike enough to carry evidence for one another. It connects to model design work around Transformers and language-model-inspired sequence processing, but with a warning: a representation borrowed from text can be poorly matched to regular web data if it breaks cross-time structure too early.
638.ww: The intuitive reason Time-TK should work is that it moves an important decision earlier in the pipeline. If the input description already preserves offset relationships, the forecasting model starts with evidence arranged in the same shape as the problem. A daily traffic pattern does not have to be rebuilt from isolated moments; pieces of the sequence that belong together across a time gap are represented as related from the start. MI-KAN can then specialize in learning offset-specific temporal patterns, while MOTI lets those patterns exchange information before the forecast is produced. This is better than the naive recipe because the naive recipe asks a later model to compensate for a representation that may have already damaged the signal. The abstract's reconstruction bound matters here because it gives a principled reason to suspect that ordinary token-style descriptions have a ceiling: even a strong downstream model cannot fully use structure that the representation did not preserve. The approach fits regular web data because repeated offsets are common enough to be useful evidence.
638.po: The payoff is more accurate forecasting for web-related time series where stable operation depends on seeing future load, flow, or throughput before it arrives. The abstract reports experiments on 14 real-world datasets, including traffic flow and BTC/USDT throughput, and says Time-TK outperforms baseline models. MOTE is also presented as a universal building block that can be integrated into different existing models, so the contribution is not only one architecture. Practically, the paper buys a way to improve long-sequence forecasting by repairing the first representation step, where a lot of useful temporal information can otherwise be lost.
638.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The time series must contain useful multi-offset temporal correlations; if the future is driven by sudden outside events that are absent from the history, preserving offsets will not solve the problem. The approach also assumes that the selected offsets and learned sub-sequences capture the right regularities rather than spurious repetition. The abstract reports broad benchmark performance but does not prove reliability under every domain change, sensor failure, market shock, or deployment constraint. It also names MI-KAN and MOTI without enough detail in the input file to verify their exact internal design. The strongest supported claim is narrower: independent time-step descriptions can bottleneck regular long sequences, and MOTE plus Time-TK is proposed to reduce that loss.

639.bp: Online shops and video platforms constantly add new products, clips, or posts. Many of these new items already have content signals, such as images, text, audio, or other media, but they have no click, watch, purchase, or rating history yet. A recommender still has to decide who might like them before the crowd has supplied evidence. This paper serves that cold-start moment. The real object is not just an item; it is a new item described by several kinds of content, a target user with a history, and other users whose past behavior may or may not reveal the same taste. The need is practical: if new items cannot be recommended early, platforms over-show old items with known histories and bury fresh inventory. SuperG tries to make early recommendation less blind by borrowing evidence from users who appear to have consistent preferences similar to the target user, then selecting the behaviors that actually help judge the new item.
639.wh: The hard part is that two shortages happen at once. First, the new item has no interaction history, so the system cannot count who clicked it or which users eventually liked it. Second, the older history around other items is noisy. A user may click by accident, follow a trend, inspect an item without liking it, or interact with something for a reason that does not transfer to a new item. It is tempting to borrow from users who co-occur with the target user on past items, but co-occurrence can be accidental. Two users may both click a popular video while having different stable tastes. The abstract calls these spurious neighbors: people who look related because of surface overlap, not because their preferences are truly consistent. Multi-modal content adds another tension. Images, text, and other media can help describe new items, but the useful behavior must still be chosen from histories where many actions are weak or misleading.
639.naive: A smart beginner would collect the target user's past interactions, find other users who clicked some of the same old items, and recommend new items whose multi-modal content resembles items clicked by that group. This is reasonable because user overlap often carries taste information, and content can stand in for missing interaction counts. The failure is that overlap is too crude. Popular items create many false neighbors. Some past interactions say little about stable preference. Treating every click from a nearby user as useful can make the system borrow noise at exactly the moment when the new item has no direct evidence to correct it. The result is a recommendation built from convenient history rather than informative history.
639.ap: SuperG's central move is to split borrowing into two questions instead of treating all nearby history as evidence. The first question is: which existing users have preferences that are genuinely similar to the target user's preferences? The similar user exploration module is meant to answer that by looking for consistency in preference signals, not merely simple co-occurrence. The second question is: once those users are found, which behaviors from their histories should guide a new-item recommendation? The informative behavior mining module retrieves useful behaviors from both the target user's own history and the histories of similar users. Finally, the behavior-guided hybrid recommendation module uses those retrieved signals together with the new item's multi-modal content to rank new items. The method is therefore not just content matching and not just neighbor borrowing. It is a filter for whom to trust, then a filter for which actions from trusted people should matter.
639.mech: The input is a target user, newly introduced items with multi-modal content, and historical interaction records from existing users and items. Because the new item has no interaction data, the system cannot start from direct item popularity or prior user feedback on that item. SuperG first examines historical preference evidence to explore users who resemble the target user. In plain terms, it asks which people have acted in ways that suggest a stable taste pattern close to this target person, rather than which people merely touched one or two of the same common items. After that, the method mines behaviors from two sources: the target user's own past actions and the past actions of users judged similar. Mining here means selecting actions that carry useful information for judging future interest, while reducing the influence of actions that look accidental, weak, or caused by broad popularity. Those selected behaviors become guidance signals. The final hybrid recommendation step combines this behavior guidance with the content of the new item across its available media. It then scores candidate new items for the target user and produces a ranked recommendation list. The abstract does not reveal the exact scoring formula, but it does make the pipeline clear: identify trustworthy similar users, retrieve informative behaviors, combine those behaviors with multi-modal item content, and use the result to recommend new items.
639.math: The main mathematical ideas are similarity, ranking, and learned weighting of evidence. Similarity means deciding when two users are close enough in preference that one user's history can inform the other user's recommendation. The important issue is what counts as close. A crude distance based on shared clicks can confuse common exposure with shared taste. SuperG's similar user exploration is a way to build a better comparison, where consistent preferences are intended to matter more than accidental co-occurrence. Ranking means turning many candidate new items into an order for the target user. Since only a few items can be shown, the model must assign scores that place more promising new items above weaker ones. Informative behavior mining is a weighting problem: not every historical action should count equally, so the system must give more influence to behaviors that help predict interest and less influence to behaviors likely to be noise. Multi-modal recommendation also uses fusion, which means combining different descriptions of the same item, such as visual and textual signals, into a decision. The tradeoff is reach versus trust: borrowing from many histories gives more evidence for new items, but each borrowed action can introduce noise unless similarity and behavior usefulness are measured carefully.
639.dots: This paper sits in the recommender-systems family because it is about choosing a small useful set from a huge and changing pile. It connects most directly to cold-start recommendation: the item exists, but the normal user-response evidence has not arrived. It also connects to similarity, because the key question is which users should be treated as neighbors, and to ranking, because the final product is an ordered list of new items. Within multimodal recommendation, it is close to papers that combine images, text, and behavior to understand item meaning, but it adds a specific pressure: content is available while interaction history is missing. It also touches the conference's recurring noise problem. Many systems have lots of data, but not all data deserves equal trust. SuperG's answer is to repair the evidence before ranking: first avoid spurious neighbors, then avoid uninformative behaviors, then let the remaining behavior guide the new-item decision.
639.ww: The mechanism should help because it attacks the two places where the naive method loses reliability. When a new item has no interactions, some borrowing is necessary; otherwise the system has only item content and the target user's private history. But borrowing from the wrong users is harmful. By searching for users with consistent similar preferences, SuperG tries to make borrowed histories more like evidence from people whose choices would plausibly transfer to the target user. The second improvement is behavior selection. Even a truly similar user has a mixed history: some actions reflect durable taste, while others reflect curiosity, trend following, or weak interest. Mining informative behaviors reduces the chance that the recommendation is steered by low-value actions. The hybrid final step matters because new items are not blank. Their images, text, or other media carry clues about what they are. If selected behaviors indicate which kinds of content similar users tend to value, then multi-modal content becomes more useful: it can be read through the lens of trustworthy preference evidence rather than scored in isolation.
639.po: The payoff is a recommender that can handle rapidly appearing new items more effectively than methods that rely on simple co-occurring signals. According to the abstract, SuperG combines similar user exploration, informative behavior mining, and behavior-guided hybrid recommendation, then outperforms state-of-the-art models on three real datasets under the multi-modal new item recommendation setting. In practical terms, this buys earlier exposure for new items and more targeted recommendations for users before direct feedback has accumulated. It also gives the platform a way to use existing histories more selectively, instead of letting every old click or every surface neighbor influence the decision.
639.limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. SuperG depends on historical interactions containing enough stable preference signal to identify truly similar users. If the logs mostly reflect exposure bias, promotion, popularity, or short-lived trends, similar user exploration may still find misleading neighbors. Informative behavior mining also assumes that useful behaviors can be separated from noisy ones from the available records. The abstract does not specify the exact model details, the modalities used in each dataset, or whether the gains hold when item content is missing, low quality, or adversarially polished. It reports empirical success on three real datasets, but that does not prove the method will transfer unchanged to every platform, domain, or pace of new-item creation.

640.bp: A temporal knowledge graph is a changing record of facts: entities are connected by named relations, and each fact belongs to a time history. A system may want to predict what event is likely to happen next, such as which entity will take part in a future relation, by looking at what has happened before. This paper serves that forecasting problem. The real object is not a single past fact, but a moving web of events where nearby facts and faraway historical patterns can both matter. DHHGN starts from the claim that good temporal reasoning needs two kinds of memory. Local history says what has recently happened around the entities involved. Global history says which older facts elsewhere in the graph may be pivotal for the prediction. The paper tries to keep both, while avoiding two failures: local graph methods that only combine one-hop neighbor evidence, and global history methods that pull in irrelevant old facts.
640.wh: The hard part is that future events in a temporal knowledge graph can depend on more than direct neighbors. A simple graph model passes information along ordinary links: an entity receives evidence from entities connected to it. That is useful for low-order structure, meaning relations that can be understood through a small neighborhood. But some event patterns are high-order: the clue is not just that A linked to B, but that several entities and facts together form a repeated interaction pattern. Ordinary pairwise edges can make this group structure hard to see. Time adds another difficulty. The graph has a large historical record, but not every old fact helps the next prediction. If a global memory mechanism treats many past facts as potentially useful, it may give attention, meaning decision weight, to irrelevant history. The model then has too much evidence, but the evidence is mixed with distractions that interfere with the event being predicted.
640.naive: A smart beginner would take all previous facts, build a normal graph from them, and run a graph neural network, meaning a learned neighbor-averaging process, over that graph. They might then feed the sequence of graph snapshots into a recurrent model, meaning a model that carries a running memory through time, and use the final state to score future facts. This is sensible because events often repeat locally and recent neighbors often matter. It fails when the useful clue is a group pattern spread across several related facts, because ordinary neighbor aggregation mostly moves evidence along pairwise links. It also fails when the historical store is too broad. More history is not automatically better if unrelated past facts receive enough weight to distort the prediction.
640.ap: DHHGN's central move is to give temporal reasoning two controlled history channels. For local history, it does not choose between an ordinary graph and a hypergraph. A hypergraph is a graph-like structure where one link can join more than two things, so it can represent a whole interaction pattern among multiple entities or facts. DHHGN uses a hybrid hypergraph-graph recurrent convolution module: the ordinary graph side keeps direct neighbor evidence, while the hypergraph side keeps higher-order group evidence. A gate, which is a learned mixing switch, decides how much each side should contribute. For global history, the dual history enhancement module tries to emphasize pivotal historical facts while still integrating the broader context. The key idea is selective memory: keep local and global evidence, but give the model machinery for deciding which form of history deserves influence for the current prediction.
640.mech: The input is a temporal knowledge graph: a sequence of historical facts, where facts connect entities through relations over time. For a prediction task, DHHGN first looks at local history around the entities and relations involved. One local view is an ordinary graph view, where facts are represented through pairwise connections and information is passed through neighborhoods. This captures low-order evidence: direct or near-direct patterns such as an entity repeatedly taking part in a relation with related entities. In parallel, DHHGN builds a hypergraph view. In that view, a single connection can bind a larger set of related entities or facts, so evidence can move through group interactions rather than only through one edge at a time. The hybrid recurrent convolution module updates these views over time, so the model carries a changing memory rather than a frozen snapshot. A learned gate then blends the graph contribution and the hypergraph contribution; the blend can favor direct-neighbor evidence when that is enough, or favor group-pattern evidence when the future event depends on a higher-order relation. Separately, the global history module reviews broader historical facts. Its dual enhancement is described as both amplifying pivotal facts and preserving holistic context, so it must score which old facts deserve extra weight while still retaining a summary of the whole past. The final representation is used to score candidate future facts and return a prediction.
640.math: The mathematical objects are graphs, hypergraphs, sequences, learned scoring, and weighted mixing. In an ordinary graph, entities or facts are nodes and pairwise links say which pieces of evidence are connected. A graph convolution is a repeated averaging-and-transforming step: each node updates its description by collecting messages from neighbors, then changing those messages into a form useful for prediction. This fits direct relational evidence but compresses a group relation into many pairwise steps. A hypergraph changes the shape of the object. Its links can connect several pieces at once, so it can represent a group dependency without pretending the group is only a set of separate pairs. Recurrent modeling handles time by carrying a memory from earlier snapshots into later ones; the risk is that old information can either be forgotten too quickly or carried forward when it no longer matters. The gate is a learned weight, a number between alternatives that decides how much graph evidence and hypergraph evidence enter the update. Global history attention is weighted selection: old facts are not all counted equally. The central tradeoff is completeness versus interference. The model wants enough history to see long patterns, but enough selectivity to keep unrelated facts from overwhelming the current event.
640.dots: This paper sits in the knowledge-graph family beside DSTAG and continual knowledge graph work in the repo. DSTAG also targets temporal knowledge graph completion and worries that evolving graphs need more than plain neighbor passing; it adds semantic tags and dual graph interaction. DHHGN attacks a nearby structural problem: local history may require higher-order group links, not only richer labels. The PyKEEN continual knowledge graph paper is related at the infrastructure level because it treats knowledge graphs as changing objects rather than fixed datasets, though its focus is updating stored number representations rather than forecasting future events. DHHGN also connects to recurring conference ideas around graph reasoning, sequence modeling, ranking, and attention. The common pressure is deciding which evidence should travel through a network and which history should influence a prediction. Its distinct answer is to split evidence by shape, using ordinary graph links for direct relations and hypergraph links for group dependencies.
640.ww: The mechanism should improve over the naive approach because it separates two questions that are easy to confuse. The first question is about shape: what kind of local dependency is present? If a future event mostly follows from direct neighboring facts, ordinary graph message passing is appropriate. If the clue appears only when several entities or facts are considered as a unit, a hypergraph can carry that group signal more directly. The gate matters because neither structure is always right. A fixed choice would overtrust one view; an adaptive blend lets the model vary the balance by context. The second question is about historical relevance. A global history module that merely collects old facts can add noise, but DHHGN's dual enhancement is designed to raise the influence of pivotal facts while keeping a whole-history background. That pairing is plausible because prediction needs both sharp clues and broad context. The paper is essentially trying to reduce two kinds of information loss: losing group interactions during local aggregation, and losing focus when global history becomes a cluttered archive.
640.po: The payoff is a temporal knowledge graph reasoner designed to make better future-event predictions from both local and global history. According to the abstract, DHHGN captures low-order neighborhood information and high-order interaction patterns at the same time, then uses a gate to blend them. It also enhances global history by emphasizing pivotal past facts while integrating all historical context. The abstract says extensive experiments on four public benchmarks validate the method, though the provided text is cut off before giving dataset names or numerical results. In practical terms, the capability is more selective event forecasting over changing facts: the system can use direct neighbors, group dependencies, and broad historical memory without treating them as the same kind of evidence.
640.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The temporal knowledge graph must contain real repeated structure, so past local and global facts are informative about future events. The hypergraph construction must group facts in a meaningful way; if the groups are noisy, high-order message passing can spread wrong evidence faster. The gate must learn when to trust graph evidence versus hypergraph evidence, which requires enough training examples covering both cases. The global history module assumes pivotal facts can be identified from the available history without overemphasizing coincidences. The abstract is truncated and does not show the exact scoring formula, hypergraph construction rule, benchmark names, numerical gains, runtime cost, or failure analysis, so those details cannot be claimed from the input.

641.bp: Many web and data-mining problems are graph problems: accounts connect to accounts, papers cite papers, products co-occur with products, and facts point to other facts. A graph model tries to give each node or whole graph a useful summary by mixing what an item says about itself with what its neighbors say around it. E2SGNN serves the version of this task where computation cost matters. Spiking neural networks replace many continuous values with binary pulses, like on/off messages sent across time. That can save energy and time because the machine mostly adds incoming pulses instead of doing many expensive multiplication-and-addition calculations. The difficulty is that graph analysis needs nuance: not all neighbors matter equally, and local neighborhood detail can differ from the broad structure of the whole graph. This paper asks whether a graph system can keep the efficiency advantage of spikes while still carrying enough detail to separate meaningfully different graph patterns.
641.wh: The hard part is the clash between two needs that pull in opposite directions. Spiking signals are cheap because each signal is mostly a binary event: a pulse happened or it did not. But that same simplicity makes them less expressive, because a continuous value can say "a little," "medium," or "strong," while a binary pulse says much less at one moment. Graph data makes the loss sharper. A node's meaning is shaped by its own content, nearby neighbors, and broader graph structure, and those sources can disagree. Existing spiking graph models therefore face an uncomfortable choice described in the abstract. They can add many real-valued multiplication-addition operations to recover detail, but then they give up the core efficiency benefit. Or they can use high-latency encoding, giving the system more time steps to express information, but then delay grows. E2SGNN is hard because it must improve expression without smuggling back the expensive computation it was meant to avoid.
641.naive: A smart beginner would first take an ordinary graph neural network and replace its messages with spikes. Each node would collect pulses from its neighbors, add them up, and pass the result through more graph layers. That preserves the low-cost flavor, but it fails when binary pulses cannot distinguish subtle neighbor differences. Another beginner would fix this by attaching continuous weights, extra real-valued calculations, or many more time steps. That may recover accuracy, but it breaks the reason for using spikes: the system again spends too much time or arithmetic on each graph. A third simple plan would give every graph the same number of processing steps. That wastes latency on easy graphs and may still underserve hard graphs.
641.ap: E2SGNN's central move is to add just enough continuous guidance to the spiking graph process, and to do it at two scales. The paper's dual-scale modulated spiking backbone keeps the main graph convolution spike-based, so neighbor messages can still be handled with low-latency, addition-only operations. Around that backbone, it injects global and local real-valued graph modulations. Local modulation helps the model notice fine neighbor-level differences: which nearby nodes matter, and how their content should shape the current node. Global modulation gives a broader graph-level adjustment, so the model is not trapped in only immediate pulse counts. The second move is latency-dynamic optimization: instead of forcing every graph through the same number of spiking steps, the system adapts latency according to data complexity. The concrete idea is to spend expressive effort where the graph needs it, while avoiding redundant time on simpler inputs.
641.mech: The input is graph data: nodes with content, links that define neighborhoods, and a task that needs a representation of the graph or its parts. E2SGNN first feeds this connected structure into a spiking graph backbone. In ordinary graph convolution, a node repeatedly gathers information from its neighbors and combines it with its own state. Here, the gathered messages are encoded through spikes, so the main communication is made of binary pulse events across a small number of time steps. If the model used only those pulses, it would risk treating different neighbor situations too similarly. The dual-scale modulation changes that calculation. A local real-valued modulation adjusts the spike-based neighbor aggregation around each node, so nearby content can influence which neighbor evidence is emphasized. A global real-valued modulation brings in wider graph information, so the representation can reflect larger structure rather than only immediate contacts. These modulations are integrated into the spiking graph convolution rather than added as a heavy separate continuous network. The result is a graph representation that keeps more discriminative content while retaining the low-latency, addition-heavy character of spiking computation. Then the latency-dynamic module estimates how complex each graph data instance is and customizes the number of processing steps. Simple graphs can stop with fewer steps; harder graphs receive more time. The output is an expressive graph representation produced under a computation budget that varies with input difficulty.
641.math: The first mathematical idea is network evidence movement. The graph is a map: nodes are items, edges are relationships, and each node carries signals about its own content. A graph convolution is a repeated rule for letting evidence travel from neighbors into a node's current summary. The danger is over-simplifying that travel. If every neighbor pulse is treated too coarsely, different neighborhoods collapse into similar summaries. The second idea is binary coding over time. A spike is a cheap on/off signal; information is represented by when pulses appear and how they accumulate. This trades detail for efficiency: fewer continuous numbers and fewer multiplications, but less room to express small differences. E2SGNN's modulation is a controlled correction to that tradeoff. Local modulation changes how immediate neighbor evidence is shaped, while global modulation changes the calculation using broader graph context. In plain terms, the model keeps the cheap pulse language but uses continuous guide rails to keep important distinctions from disappearing. The latency module uses constrained optimization: it chooses how many time steps to spend on each graph so the cost of delay is not fixed blindly. The score being balanced is expression versus efficiency. More time and real-valued adjustment can help the answer, but too much destroys the spiking advantage.
641.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of graph learning, efficient systems, and spiking neural networks. In the repo's current map, it is close to the network concept because it relies on evidence moving through graph links: neighbors help define a node or graph, but the method must decide how that evidence should be shaped. It is also close to optimization because the latency-dynamic module treats computation time as a scarce resource to allocate differently across graph inputs. Compared with MASI, another spiking paper in the repo data, E2SGNN is less about fitting inference into changing edge-device memory and more about making graph representations expressive without losing spike efficiency. Compared with SIGHT, a spiking graph paper about uncertainty under changing graph data, E2SGNN focuses on the expression-efficiency tradeoff inside the representation itself. The broader conference pattern is that many papers choose between richer modeling and practical cost; this one makes that tradeoff explicit for connected data and pulse-based computation.
641.ww: The mechanism should improve over the naive spike-only graph model because it repairs the exact place where spike-only processing loses information. A binary pulse can be cheap and useful, but it cannot by itself carry every shade of neighbor importance or graph context at one instant. Local modulation gives the spiking convolution a way to treat nearby graph evidence differently when nearby content deserves different treatment. Global modulation helps because some graph distinctions are not visible from one node's immediate neighborhood; larger structure can change what a local pattern means. Since these modulations are integrated into the spiking process, the system does not need to retreat fully to heavy continuous arithmetic. The latency-dynamic module helps for a separate reason. A fixed number of time steps assumes all graph inputs require the same amount of evidence accumulation. If some graphs are simple, that fixed schedule wastes time; if others are complex, it may spend time in the wrong uniform way. Customizing latency aligns computation with data difficulty. The claimed experiments showing better expression and efficiency are plausible if these two savings remove different failures: lost detail in representation and redundant time in processing.
641.po: The payoff is a spiking graph neural network that aims to be both expressive and efficient instead of choosing only one side. According to the abstract, E2SGNN can generate graph representations with stronger content expressiveness while keeping low-latency and addition-only efficiency advantages. It also reduces latency redundancy by adapting the number of processing steps to graph complexity. In practical terms, this buys a graph analysis tool for settings where connected data is large or time-sensitive and where ordinary continuous graph models may be too costly. The abstract reports experiments on various datasets demonstrating superiority in both expression and efficiency, though it does not give the detailed numbers here.
641.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The graph's links and node content must carry useful signal, because no modulation can fix a graph whose relationships are misleading for the task. The local and global real-valued modulations must be lightweight enough that they do not erase the savings from spike-based addition. The data-complexity estimate used for dynamic latency must reliably tell easy graphs from hard ones; otherwise the model may stop too early or waste time anyway. The abstract says experiments cover various datasets, but it does not specify which graph types, hardware settings, or latency measurements are decisive. It also does not prove that the same tradeoff will hold for every large real-world deployment.

642.bp: A recommender system constantly makes small choices for people: which product, article, coupon, video, or restaurant to show next. Teams want to know whether a new choice rule would do better before they risk showing it to real users. Off-policy evaluation is the offline version of that question. It asks: using logs collected by an older system, can we estimate how a different system would have performed? This paper revisits that evaluation problem for contextual bandits, where each decision has a situation, an action, and later feedback such as a click or reward. The practical need is clear: online experiments cost traffic, money, and user patience, while offline comparisons can be run many times. The paper studies inverse propensity score methods, which reweight old logged events to imitate the new policy being tested. Its main concern is not inventing another estimator, but asking whether conclusions from these estimators remain stable when the evaluation pipeline changes.
642.wh: The hard part is that logs are not neutral records of user preference. They are records of what a previous recommendation policy chose to expose. If the old system rarely showed an item in a certain situation, the log contains little evidence about how users would have reacted to that item there. Inverse propensity scoring tries to correct this by using the probability that the old system took each logged action. But the correction can become fragile. Rare logged actions receive large weights, so a small number of events can pull an estimate strongly. The abstract says rankings of estimators change with random seeds, log generators, and sample size, even in synthetic environments. Real logs add another difficulty: they may not behave like independent repeated draws from one fixed process. The Open Bandit Dataset analysis points to logging behavior and data characteristics that may violate that clean assumption.
642.naive: A smart beginner would take the historical log, replay each candidate policy on it, and average the rewards for the cases where the policy's preferred action matches the action that was actually logged. That seems fair because it uses only observed outcomes, not guesses. It fails because the matching cases are not a balanced sample of all situations. They are filtered through the old logging policy. A new policy may favor actions the old policy almost never tried, leaving too little evidence. Another naive move is to trust a single synthetic simulator because it gives clean ground truth. The paper warns that even synthetic rankings can flip when the seed, data size, or log generator changes.
642.ap: The paper's core move is to treat off-policy evaluation as an empirical object that depends on the whole pipeline, not only on the formula for an estimator. It focuses on inverse propensity score methods and their modifications, then asks how conclusions change when the surrounding choices change. The important output is a ranking of estimators: which evaluation method appears best under a given setup. The paper shows that this ranking is itself unstable. That matters because researchers and practitioners often compare evaluation schemes in synthetic environments and then infer that one scheme is safer or more accurate. This paper presses on that inference. It compares how results depend on random seeds, log generators, and sample size, and it examines Open Bandit Dataset logs for behavior that may break the independent-and-identically-distributed story assumed by standard log generation.
642.mech: The mechanism begins with logged bandit data. Each record contains a context, such as information about a user or recommendation moment; an action chosen by the logging policy; a reward or response; and the probability that the logging policy assigned to that action. A candidate evaluation method then tries to estimate how well a target policy would have done. In inverse propensity scoring, a logged event matters most when the target policy would also choose or strongly favor the logged action. The observed reward is then divided by the logging probability. In plain terms, if the old system rarely chose this action but it happened and produced a reward, that event stands in for many similar missed chances. Modifications of IPS change this weighting behavior to reduce variance, bias, or instability. The paper varies the evaluation pipeline around these estimators. In synthetic environments, it changes random seeds, the process that generated the logged actions, and the number of samples. For each setup, estimators are scored and ranked. The reported finding is that the ranking is sensitive to those pipeline choices. The paper then turns to the Open Bandit Dataset, looking at logging behavior and data characteristics. The output is not simply one winning estimator. It is evidence that the path from data generation to estimator comparison can decide the conclusion.
642.math: The central mathematics is counterfactual estimation, which means estimating an outcome for a choice that was not actually made. The log tells us what happened under the old policy, but the question concerns a different policy. Probability enters through the propensity score: the chance that the logging policy took the action recorded in the log. Inverse propensity scoring uses that chance as a correction weight. If an action was sampled with probability one half, one observed reward counts like two such opportunities; if it was sampled with probability one hundredth, one reward counts like one hundred. This is meant to undo exposure bias, the fact that the old policy decided what evidence could be seen. The tradeoff is bias versus variance. Bias is systematic error from using a tilted log as if it were neutral. Variance is the estimate jumping around because a few heavily weighted records dominate. Sample size matters because more records can calm random jumps, but only if the records cover the actions the target policy needs. The i.i.d. assumption says records behave like independent draws from the same process. If logging behavior changes over time, users influence one another, or exposure patterns are structured, that assumption weakens and the probability correction may no longer mean what the formula says.
642.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of recommendation, ranking, probability, and repeated decision making. In the recommender-systems family, many papers try to choose a small useful set from a huge pile, but this paper asks how to judge a chooser before deploying it. It is also tied to ranking because the practical result of off-policy evaluation is often an ordered list: policy A looks better than policy B, or estimator X looks more trustworthy than estimator Y. The probability concept is central because the method turns partial logged evidence into a measured belief about unseen outcomes. It also connects to reinforcement-learning and bandit work in the repo, where actions create the feedback later used for learning. The shared difficulty is circular evidence: the system learns from data produced by earlier choices. This paper is a cautionary sibling to method-building papers, because it studies whether the measuring stick itself is stable.
642.ww: The approach works as a diagnostic because it moves attention from elegant formulas to the conditions under which those formulas are used. IPS can be correct in a clean setting because the propensity score tells how much of the world each observed action represents. If the old policy gave every relevant action some known chance of appearing, reweighting can rebuild the average reward the target policy would have seen. But if estimator rankings flip across seeds, log generators, and sample sizes, then a single reported comparison is weaker than it looks. By repeatedly changing the pipeline, the paper reveals which conclusions depend on accidental experimental choices. The Open Bandit Dataset analysis adds a reality check. Real recommender logs can contain structured logging behavior, changing exposure, or other data characteristics that do not look like independent repeated draws. Inspecting those properties explains why an estimator that behaves well in a neat simulator may not provide the same confidence on real platform data.
642.po: The payoff is a more cautious and useful way to read off-policy evaluation results. The paper shows that comparing IPS-based estimators is not only a matter of choosing a formula; it also depends on how logs are generated, how much data is available, and which random seed produced the experiment. For practitioners, this means an offline winner should not be trusted merely because it ranked first in one pipeline. For researchers, it questions validation built mainly on synthetic environments that may not share the structure of real recommender logs. The concrete capability is diagnostic: identify when evaluation conclusions are fragile before they guide deployment decisions.
642.limits: The abstract supports claims about sensitivity and assumption checks, not a universal replacement for IPS. It does not prove that every IPS modification fails, only that conclusions about their rankings can depend strongly on pipeline choices. The Open Bandit Dataset gives real logging evidence, but one benchmark cannot represent every recommender platform. The analysis also depends on knowing or estimating the logging probabilities accurately. If those propensities are wrong, the correction is built on a false scale. Finally, showing that i.i.d. assumptions may be violated does not by itself quantify the exact error for every downstream policy comparison.

643.bp: A recommender system is trying to choose the next useful item for a person from a large catalog. In this paper, each item is not described by one kind of evidence. It may have text, images, behavior records, and other item signals. The ordinary need is simple: a shopping, media, or content platform wants the next recommendation to match what this particular user is likely to want now, given the user's past sequence of choices. The difficulty is that the useful clue may not live inside any single source. A picture may suggest style, text may explain function, and past clicks may show taste, but the strongest signal can appear only when these sources are read together. PRISM serves this recommendation moment by asking how different item signals should be separated, combined, and personalized instead of fused in one fixed way for everyone.
643.wh: The hard part is that multiple item signals do not contribute independently. Some information is unique: only one source says it. Some is redundant: two sources repeat the same clue. Some is synergistic: two sources together reveal something neither source shows alone. A fixed fusion rule treats these cases too crudely. It might count repeated evidence twice, miss a cross-source clue, or force every user to care about the same signal mixture. Sequential recommendation adds another pressure because the system must read a person's ordered history and infer the next likely item, not just make a general item match. Two users can look at the same item evidence and value different combinations. One may care about visual style plus category; another may care about text description plus prior behavior. The abstract says existing models often overlook synergy and assume fixed importance across users, which is exactly where the information gets flattened.
643.naive: A smart beginner would collect every available item signal, convert each one into a comparable feature list, concatenate the lists, and train the recommender to score candidate items from the user's history. A slightly better beginner might assign a learned weight to each source, such as more weight for images or more weight for text. This fails when the useful clue is not a source by itself but a relationship between sources. If image and text repeat the same fact, adding both can overstate it. If image and behavior only become meaningful together, separate weights can miss it. It also fails personally: one shared set of weights assumes all users interpret modality combinations the same way.
643.ap: PRISM's central move is to treat fusion as an information accounting problem before it becomes a recommendation scoring problem. Instead of asking only, "How much should each modality matter?" it asks, "What part of the evidence is unique to one modality, what part is repeated across modalities, and what part appears only when modalities interact?" The Interaction Expert Layer performs this decomposition into unique, redundant, and synergistic components. Then the Adaptive Fusion Layer decides how much of each component to use for a particular user, guided by that user's preferences. The paper also frames PRISM as attachable to existing sequential recommendation models, so the core claim is not that it replaces the whole recommender. It adds a finer middle layer between raw multimodal item evidence and the final next-item ranking.
643.mech: The mechanism begins with a user's interaction sequence and item descriptions from several modalities, meaning several kinds of evidence about the same item. A sequential recommender backbone supplies the basic setting: read the user's past ordered behavior and produce signals useful for predicting what comes next. PRISM then inserts a specialized fusion step. First, the Interaction Expert Layer looks at modality interactions rather than only individual modalities. For each relevant combination, it tries to separate three roles. Unique information is evidence that one modality contributes on its own. Redundant information is the overlap where multiple modalities say essentially the same thing. Synergistic information is the extra clue that exists because modalities are considered together. Next, the Adaptive Fusion Layer uses user preference guidance to weight these pieces dynamically. The same visual-text interaction can therefore matter more for one user and less for another. After weighting, the fused representation is passed back into the sequential recommendation process, where candidate items are scored and ordered. The output is still a recommendation list, but the score is built from a more careful map of what each modality and each modality combination contributed.
643.math: The main mathematical idea is information decomposition. In plain terms, information is a measure of how much an observation reduces uncertainty. If seeing an item image narrows down what the item is, the image carries information. If the text says the same thing, some of that information is redundant. If image and text together narrow uncertainty in a way neither can alone, that is synergy. This is why the abstract calls the design information-theoretic: it treats each signal source as a carrier of uncertainty-reducing evidence and asks how that evidence overlaps or combines. The second idea is personalized weighting, which is a scoring problem. The model must choose how strongly each decomposed component should influence the recommendation for this user. The third idea is sequence modeling: the user's past actions are ordered, so the recent and earlier items provide clues about the next item. Finally, ranking turns the fused score into a practical decision by sorting candidate items. The tradeoff is detail versus reliability: separating evidence too coarsely misses synergy, but separating it too finely only helps if the decomposition is learned from enough reliable interaction data.
643.dots: This paper connects to a large recommender-systems thread in the repo: many papers are about choosing a small useful set from a huge catalog under partial evidence. It also connects to the sequence concept because the target is not a timeless preference profile but the next item after an ordered history. The information concept is especially direct: PRISM is about measuring what each modality tells the system, what it repeats, and what only appears in combination. Nearby papers in the same batch expose related pressures. SuperG handles new multimodal items by finding similar users and useful behaviors when item history is missing. MinSAR tries to bridge search intent and recommendation intent when explicit queries and implicit behavior disagree. PRISM addresses a narrower but central version of the same field problem: how to keep different evidence sources from being mashed together before the system knows which combinations matter for this user.
643.ww: The method should help because recommendation errors often come from using the right evidence in the wrong shape. If two modalities repeat a clue, a plain fusion model may treat repetition as stronger proof than it really is. If two modalities create a clue together, a source-by-source model may never see it. PRISM's decomposition gives the model named places to put these different cases, so the later scoring step can use them differently. The user-guided fusion matters because preference is not only about items; it is about which aspects of items a person responds to. A user who repeatedly chooses visually similar items should not receive the same modality mixture as a user whose history is better explained by textual category or behavior patterns. By making the weights adaptive, PRISM can let the same item evidence mean different things in different user histories. The abstract's experiments across four datasets and three sequential recommendation backbones support the claim that this inserted module is useful beyond one narrow model setup.
643.po: The payoff is finer control over multimodal sequential recommendation. Instead of improving the next-item score by simply adding more data sources, PRISM tries to explain how those sources relate before fusing them. That buys the ability to use unique evidence, avoid overcounting repeated evidence, and capture information that appears only through modality combinations. Because the abstract says PRISM is plug-and-play and tested with three sequential recommendation backbones, the practical promise is that existing recommendation models can add this information-synergy module without being rebuilt from scratch. The reported experiments on four datasets ground the claim in repeated evaluation rather than a single example.
643.limits: The abstract does not specify exactly how unique, redundant, and synergistic information are estimated, so the reliability of the decomposition cannot be judged from this input alone. The approach assumes the available modalities actually contain useful and alignable clues; if image, text, or behavior signals are noisy or mismatched, the fusion layer may confidently combine weak evidence. It also assumes user histories reveal stable enough preferences to guide adaptive weights. New users, very short histories, or fast-changing tastes may weaken personalization. The experiments cover four datasets and three backbones, but the abstract does not prove behavior in every catalog, platform, modality mix, or cold-start condition.

644.bp: Modern platforms rarely have a single doorway. A person may type a query when they know what they want, then browse recommendations when they are exploring or when the platform wants to surface useful items without being asked. Those two behaviors are different windows into the same person. Search gives explicit intent: the query says, in words, what the person is asking for now. Recommendation gives implicit intent: clicks, views, purchases, or other interactions hint at what the person tends to like, even when no query is present. This paper serves platforms where search and recommendation must work together instead of behaving like separate products. The title and abstract frame the need as joint search-recommendation modeling: a system should understand long-term user preferences, short-term context, and search queries in one coherent interest picture, so the search channel and the browsing channel can help each other rather than pulling the user model in different directions.
644.wh: The hard part is that the two channels speak different languages. A query is direct but narrow: it captures what the user typed at one moment, and it may miss the user's longer history. Behavioral interactions are broad but indirect: they show what the user did, but not always why. A person might search for one product because of a temporary need while their past behavior points toward a different category. Existing joint search-recommendation models, according to the abstract, suffer from cross-scenario interest inconsistency: they fail to turn explicit search intent and implicit recommendation intent into a coherent user interest representation. The second difficulty is the trade-off between tasks. If the model shares knowledge statically, the search side may dominate the recommendation side, or the reverse. Features useful for semantic matching in search are not always the same as features useful for collaborative filtering in recommendation, so improving one task can degrade the other.
644.naive: A smart beginner would first build two separate systems: one search model that matches the user's query to items, and one recommendation model that learns from past interactions. If forced to combine them, the beginner might concatenate the query signal, the user history, and recent behavior into one large user vector, then feed the same shared representation to both tasks. That fails for two reasons named in the abstract. First, it does not decide which signals express the same underlying interest and which are temporary or channel-specific. Second, it treats sharing as fixed. Search and recommendation do not always need the same information in the same amount, so a fixed shared block can create task conflict instead of cooperation.
644.ap: MinSAR's core move is to generate a unified interest before deciding how search and recommendation should use it. The paper introduces a Unified Interest Generation module that combines long-term preferences from a user-specific memory network with short-term contextual behaviors. It uses VQ-VAE, which can be understood as a learned compression system: many messy behavior and query signals are mapped into a smaller set of learned interest codes, so the model must express the user's state through compact reusable patterns rather than an unlimited, noisy description. That generated interest is then used to guide an Interest-Guided Attention Expert Network. Here, attention means assigning different amounts of weight to different expert parts of the model. The experts include shared knowledge across search and recommendation, plus task-specific expertise for semantic matching in search and collaborative filtering in recommendation.
644.mech: The mechanism starts with the platform's evidence about a user. One stream is long-term preference: the user's accumulated behavior is stored through a user-specific memory network, which acts like a personalized record of recurring interests. Another stream is short-term context: recent actions around the current moment, which may show a temporary need or a fresh browsing direction. Search also has explicit intent through the query, while recommendation has implicit intent through interactions. The Unified Interest Generation module brings these streams together. It passes them through a VQ-VAE, a model that learns to encode inputs, snap them to a limited codebook of interest patterns, and decode or use those patterns downstream. The important mechanical effect is compression plus alignment: different surface signals must land on a shared set of interest codes if they point to the same user need. Once this unified interest exists, the Interest-Guided Attention Expert Network uses it as a control signal. Instead of giving every task the same shared features, it allocates weights among shared knowledge and task-specific experts. For search, the relevant expert focuses on semantic matching, meaning whether a query and an item mean compatible things. For recommendation, the relevant expert focuses on collaborative filtering, meaning using behavior patterns across users and items. The output is task predictions for search and recommendation shaped by one interest signal but not forced through one rigid pathway.
644.math: The first mathematical idea is representation learning, which means learning a reusable description of the user from examples rather than hand-writing rules such as "recent clicks matter twice as much as old clicks." In this paper, the representation is meant to join explicit and implicit intent. The second idea is quantized compression. VQ-VAE uses a codebook: instead of allowing every user state to become an arbitrary point, it maps the state to one of many learned interest codes. In everyday terms, it is like forcing messy evidence into a vocabulary of recurring taste patterns. That can remove noise, but it also risks losing detail if the codebook is too coarse. The third idea is multi-task learning, where one system learns search and recommendation together. The trade-off is shared strength versus interference: shared parts help when both tasks use the same evidence, but hurt when each task needs different evidence. The fourth idea is weighted allocation. The attention expert network scores how much each expert should matter for the current unified interest. This is a form of optimization: the model changes its internal weights during training to reduce wrong search and recommendation predictions while learning when to share and when to specialize.
644.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of information retrieval and recommender systems. Search papers often ask how to rank items against an explicit request; recommendation papers often ask how to rank items when the request is hidden inside behavior. MinSAR treats those as two versions of the same deeper problem: infer what the user wants from incomplete evidence, then sort possible items accordingly. It also connects to similarity, because both semantic matching and collaborative filtering depend on deciding what should count as close: close in meaning for query-item pairs, or close in behavior for users and items. It connects to learning from examples because the unified interest codes are not hand-defined categories; they are learned from platform data. Within the batch, it is near papers about multimodal sequential recommendation and cold-start recommendation, because all ask how to combine weak, partial signals into a user state that can guide ranking.
644.ww: The approach should help when the same underlying interest is visible through different channels but not in the same form. A query may say "Kindle mystery novels," while past interactions may show preferred authors, price ranges, or reading habits. Separate systems cannot easily connect those clues. A single flat shared model can connect them, but it may over-share and make the search task absorb recommendation noise or make recommendation chase the literal query. MinSAR's generated interest gives the model a middle layer: first infer the user state, then let each task use that state differently. Quantized codes can make this middle layer steadier by grouping similar intent patterns, so small behavior differences do not always create unrelated user descriptions. The attention expert network then reduces the task trade-off by making sharing conditional. If the current interest needs common knowledge, shared experts get more weight; if search or recommendation needs its own skill, task-specific experts can receive more weight.
644.po: The payoff is a joint search-recommendation model that aims to reduce two failures named in the abstract: inconsistent user interests across scenarios and a severe trade-off where improving one channel hurts the other. The paper claims MinSAR bridges explicit queries and implicit behavioral interactions through compact cross-scenario interest representations, then uses those interests to balance shared and task-specific knowledge. The abstract also says the method is evaluated on two real-world datasets, KuaiSAR and Amazon Kindle Store. Because the provided abstract cuts off before concrete result details, the strongest grounded claim is about the capability: a platform can model search and recommendation as coordinated views of one user interest rather than separate prediction jobs.
644.limits: The method assumes that explicit search intent and implicit recommendation intent often come from a recoverable shared interest. That will not always hold: a user can search for a gift, perform work-related research, or browse out of curiosity, all of which may conflict with long-term personal preference. The quantized interest codes also assume useful interests can be compressed without discarding crucial details. If the codebook is poorly learned or too small, different needs may be merged. The attention expert network assumes training data is rich enough to learn when to share and when to specialize. The abstract names datasets but does not provide the missing result details here, so it does not prove general deployment reliability, fairness across user groups, or behavior under sudden changes in user intent.
